Above Ollantaytambo, where the Sacred Valley of the Incas narrows, a side valley climbs north toward the high passes of the Urubamba range, following the Patacancha river. The segment between Patacancha and Huacahuasi is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system, and it crosses some of the most beautiful country in the Cusco region: steep slopes covered with potato fields and terraces, small villages of stone and adobe houses, herds of llamas and alpacas grazing in high pastures, and snow-capped peaks above. The communities of this area, like Patacancha and Huacahuasi, are known for their weaving, with intricate designs and bright colours, and the women's traditional dress is among the most striking in the Andes.

This is the route of the Lares trek, an alternative to the classic Inca Trail, which passes through remote villages and over high passes, and many visitors choose it to experience the living culture of the Andes. Huacahuasi has hot springs that are a welcome reward after a day of walking or riding.

The road up the Patacancha valley from Ollantaytambo is mostly unpaved, a dirt track that climbs steadily with switchbacks and river crossings, reaching altitudes above four thousand metres. It is a demanding but rewarding ride, best suited to light adventure bikes. Altitude is a serious factor, so acclimatise in Cusco or the Sacred Valley before going higher. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time to ride, with clear skies and firm roads; the rainy season brings mud and landslides.

Urubamba, about twenty-one kilometres away, is the nearest town with full services, including fuel, shops and restaurants, and Ollantaytambo, at the mouth of the valley, has a spectacular Inca fortress and temple and plenty of restaurants and hotels. In the villages, you may find small shops selling basic supplies, but carry food, water and extra fuel. The people are generally welcoming, and buying textiles directly from the weavers is a great way to support the community. Respect local customs and always ask before taking photographs of people.
t.tchogha zanbil@32.0,48.5:
Around 1250 BC, a king of Elam called Untash-Napirisha built a holy city in the plain of what is now Khuzestan in south-western Iran, and at its centre he raised a ziggurat, a stepped temple tower, to the god Inshushinak. Chogha Zanbil, as it is now called, is one of the best-preserved ziggurats anywhere, its millions of mud bricks still standing in great tiers above the flat land, some stamped with inscriptions in the Elamite script. It was the first site in Iran to be listed by UNESCO, in 1979, and it remains a powerful, almost eerie place.

The city was never finished and was later sacked by the Assyrians, but the ziggurat survived, buried and protected by its own collapse until excavations in the twentieth century. Walking around it, you see the walls of the sacred precinct, temples and the remains of an advanced water system. The size of the bricks, the precision of the walls and the inscriptions give a vivid sense of a civilisation that rivalled Babylon.

The landscape is flat, hot and wide, with the Zagros mountains rising in the distance and the Karun and Dez rivers bringing life to the plains. Riding here is mostly about long straight roads, often in intense heat, with fast-moving traffic, trucks and the occasional wandering animal. Summer temperatures in Khuzestan are among the highest on earth, often above forty-five degrees, so this is a winter destination, when days are mild and pleasant.

Shushtar and Shush, each about thirty kilometres away, are the nearest towns, with fuel, food and lodging. Shush is the site of ancient Susa, one of the great cities of the ancient world, with its excavations and a castle built by French archaeologists in the nineteenth century, as well as the tomb of the prophet Daniel. Shushtar is famous for its historic hydraulic system, a complex of dams, canals and mills that is also listed by UNESCO.

Local food includes rich stews, rice dishes and fish from the rivers, with strong flavours of herbs and spices. Come between November and March, when the weather is kindest. Visit Chogha Zanbil in the late afternoon, when the low sun turns the bricks gold and the shadows stretch across the plain, and stand in silence before a monument more than three thousand years old.
t.segment kintama tawis@-12.7,-72.0:
The Inca built a road network that stretched some thirty thousand kilometres along the Andes, from southern Colombia to central Chile, and much of it still exists as stone paths, staircases and causeways through the mountains. The Qhapaq Ñan, as it is called, was listed by UNESCO in 2014 as a set of segments across six countries. The Kintama-Tawis segment lies in the mountains north of the Sacred Valley of Cusco, in the high country between the valley and the cloud forests that descend toward the Amazon and the Manú national park.

This is a land of Quechua-speaking communities who still farm potatoes and keep llamas and alpacas at altitudes of three to four thousand metres and more, and who weave textiles in bright, intricate patterns that tell stories of their villages. The Lares area, to the west, is known for its hot springs and for treks between villages that are an alternative to the busier Inca Trail. Below, the valleys drop steeply toward the jungle, and the vegetation changes from grassland to cloud forest within a few hours' walk, with orchids, ferns and hummingbirds.

Riding here is serious business. Roads are often dirt or gravel, with steep climbs, hairpins and passes above four thousand metres, where the air is thin and the bike loses power. Landslides are common in the rainy season, from November to March, and some roads become impassable. The dry season, from May to September, has clear skies, cold nights and dusty roads. Altitude sickness is a real risk, so acclimatise in Cusco for a few days before riding high. Expect trucks, buses and livestock, and do not ride after dark.

For fuel, the towns of the Sacred Valley, such as Calca and Urubamba, are the reliable places, and you should carry extra if heading into the mountains. Food in the villages is simple: potato soups, quinoa, corn and the occasional roasted guinea pig, a local delicacy. Coca tea helps with the altitude. The Inca road itself is for walkers, not vehicles, so leave the bike in a village and walk a stretch. The stones were laid five hundred years ago, and the path still runs straight up the mountain with Inca disregard for gradients.
t.segment paucarpata ichuka@-12.9,-72.0:
North-east of Cusco, the Andes begin their great fall towards the Amazon. Somewhere in the high grassland between Paucartambo and the edge of the cloud forest, the segment of Inca road between Paucarpata and Ichuka crosses the puna, a land of tussock grass, cold lakes and rocky ridges at well over 3,500 metres. It is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, and the rides that pass here link it with the Manú National Park, one of the most biodiverse protected areas on Earth, which stretches from these heights down into lowland rainforest.

The Inca roads here connected the imperial heartland around Cusco with the warm valleys of the eastern slope, where coca, fruit and other products came from. Llama caravans carried goods up and down, and the road was maintained by local communities as part of their labour obligations to the state. Fragments of paving and stone walls survive in the grass, often still used by herders.

The approach from Cusco is through Paucartambo, a colonial town famous for its festival of the Virgen del Carmen in July, when dancers in elaborate masks fill the streets. Beyond the town, a road climbs to the ridge at Tres Cruces, famous for spectacular sunrises over the Amazon basin, and then plunges into the Kosñipata valley, dropping thousands of metres through cloud forest full of orchids, hummingbirds and the scarlet cock-of-the-rock.

This is adventure riding in its purest form. Much of the road is gravel or dirt, narrow and winding, with sheer drops, fog and rain that can turn the surface into mud. Trucks and buses use it, and passing on a single track can be tense. The dry season from May to September is the time to go, and even then afternoons in the cloud forest are often wet.

There are no services near the segment itself. Fill up in Cusco or Paucartambo, carry extra fuel and water, and be prepared for cold nights on the high ground and humid heat lower down. The combination of Inca heritage, wild landscapes and the sudden transition from puna to rainforest makes this one of the most memorable rides in Peru, provided you respect the distances and the altitude.
Shushtar sits on a rocky outcrop above the Karun, Iran's largest river, in the plains of Khuzestan, and for nearly two thousand years its people have bent that river to their will. The hydraulic system here, listed by UNESCO in 2009, is a network of dams, weirs, canals, tunnels and mills built mainly in the Sasanian era, from the third century onward, to divert water for irrigation and power. The best known element was the Band-e Kaisar, a long bridge-dam across the Karun, traditionally said to have been built by Roman prisoners captured with the Emperor Valerian at the Battle of Edessa in 260. Only fragments remain, but the story of Roman engineers working for a Persian king is one of the great footnotes of ancient history.

The most spectacular sight is the mill complex at the edge of town, where water from the Gargar canal pours through tunnels cut into the rock and cascades down a cliff in a series of waterfalls, turning the wheels of mills that once ground grain for the region. Walking among the channels, bridges and mill chambers, with the sound of rushing water everywhere, is a cool, refreshing experience in a place where heat is the dominant fact of life.

Khuzestan is one of the hottest places on earth. Summer temperatures regularly exceed forty-five degrees, sometimes fifty, and riding in that heat is dangerous. Come between November and March, when the days are warm and pleasant and the nights cool. The landscape is flat and open, with palm groves, wheat fields and the foothills of the Zagros rising to the northeast.

Shushtar is one of a cluster of ancient sites in the region. Susa, a short ride west, was one of the capitals of the Achaemenid Empire, and the tomb of the prophet Daniel stands there. Chogha Zanbil, an Elamite ziggurat from the thirteenth century BC, rises from the plain between them, one of the best preserved in the world.

The town has fuel, shops and simple restaurants. Before planning any motorcycle trip to Iran, check carefully the current travel advice, visa rules and the requirement for a carnet de passage for your bike, and be aware that international bank cards do not work, so you will need to carry cash.
t.segment chiwuanquiri@-14.4,-71.5:
The Qhapaq Ñan, the great road system of the Inca Empire, stretched over thirty thousand kilometres across the Andes, linking Cusco with the farthest corners of the empire, from southern Colombia to central Chile. In 2014, UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site across six countries, and the listing includes hundreds of individual segments, each a fragment of the network. The Chiwuanquiri segment lies in the high province of Canas, south of Cusco, near the village of Cahuanuyo, on the high puna at around four thousand metres. Here, the old road crosses open grassland, with stone paving, retaining walls and drainage channels still visible in places, and it is a moving experience to walk on a road built more than five centuries ago.

The same province is home to one of the most remarkable traditions in the Andes. The Q'eswachaka bridge, a suspension bridge woven from grass rope, spans the gorge of the Apurímac river, and every year the communities of the area gather to rebuild it by hand, using techniques passed down from the Incas. The ritual lasts several days and has been recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. If you are in the area at the right time, usually in June, it is an unforgettable sight.

The landscape is the high puna, a vast, rolling plateau of tough grass, with lakes, snow-capped peaks in the distance and herds of llamas and alpacas. The villages are small, built of adobe and stone, and the people speak Quechua as their first language. The air is thin, the sun intense, the nights freezing.

The riding is high and remote. The roads in the province are a mix of paved and unpaved, with long climbs, hairpins and variable surfaces, and they demand experience and respect. Altitude affects both rider and machine: bikes lose power, and riders can suffer from altitude sickness, so acclimatise in Cusco for several days before heading up. Weather changes quickly, with afternoon storms in the rainy season, from December to March.

Sicuani, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest town with full services, fuel and mechanics. Carry extra fuel, water, warm clothing and food, and do not underestimate the distances. Try a cup of coca tea, which helps with the altitude.
t.segment machaqmarka raqchi qquea@-14.2,-:
The Vilcanota valley south of Cusco is the old highway of the Andes, and the Inca road ran along it towards Lake Titicaca and the southern provinces of the empire. The segment between Machaqmarka, Raqchi and Qquea is one of the sections of the Qhapaq Ñan listed by UNESCO, and it passes one of the most impressive Inca sites outside Cusco. At Raqchi, near San Pedro de Cacha, the Temple of Wiracocha, dedicated to the creator god, was an enormous building with a central wall of stone and adobe that still rises around fifteen metres high, flanked by rows of columns. Around it are the remains of storehouses, the round qollqas, lined up in rows, houses, baths and fountains, and a lava field from the nearby volcano of Kinsach'ata, which according to legend erupted when Wiracocha passed by. The village holds a festival in June, with music and dancing.

The valley is also the land of Túpac Amaru II, the leader of the great indigenous rebellion of 1780 against Spanish rule. José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a local cacique who took the name of the last Inca, launched the uprising in the nearby town of Tinta, and although it was crushed and he was executed in Cusco in 1781, he remains a national hero in Peru. Tinta, Tungasuca and the villages around keep his memory alive.

The landscape is wide and green, with the Vilcanota river flowing through fields of maize, potatoes and barley, and mountains rising on both sides, some capped with snow. The villages are built of adobe, with red-tiled roofs, and the churches, like the one in Andahuaylillas further north, known as the Sistine Chapel of the Andes, are full of colonial paintings.

The riding is good. The paved highway from Cusco to Puno runs along the valley, with gentle curves, good surface and views over the river and the mountains, though trucks and buses can be heavy. The side roads to the villages are narrower, often unpaved. Altitude, around three and a half thousand metres, demands acclimatisation, and the weather can change quickly.

Sicuani, about eighteen kilometres away, has fuel, mechanics and restaurants, and the villages along the highway have small shops. Try chicha de jora, a fermented maize drink, in a village bar marked by a red flag.
t.segment inca mach ay samarinapata@-13.2,:
This is a stretch of the Inca road, and it is made for feet. The Qhapaq Ñan was the great road system of the Inca empire, more than thirty thousand kilometres of stone causeways, steps, bridges and tunnels linking the Pacific coast to the high Andes and from Colombia down to Chile and Argentina. UNESCO listed the network across six countries in 2014. The segment between Mach'ay and Samarinapata runs through the mountains of the Cusco region, west of Machu Picchu, and its name tells the story. A mach'ay is a cave, and samarina is a place to rest, so the route marks shelters and stopping points for travellers and for the chasquis, the relay runners who carried messages and goods at great speed across the empire.

You will not ride the trail itself, which is a narrow path of stone paving over passes above four thousand metres, but the valleys around it make a fine day on a motorbike. The Urubamba valley road from Cusco through Urubamba and Ollantaytambo is smooth, and further on it climbs toward the Abra Málaga pass, high above four thousand metres, with hairpins, cloud forest and a dramatic drop into the jungle on the far side. The surface is good, but landslides, cold fog and sudden rain are common, and altitude can make a rider dizzy, so take it slowly, drink water and give yourself a couple of days in Cusco to acclimatise.

I do not know the exact spot of this segment and prefer to say so, since route names in the Inca network are often local and the tracks are dispersed. Fuel is available in Cusco, Urubamba and Ollantaytambo, but not in the high villages, so fill up before you leave the valley. Small shops sell water, snacks and coca tea, and Quechua-speaking families still herd llamas and alpacas on the high pastures.

The dry season, from May to September, brings clear days and cold nights, and the rainy months, from November to March, bring mud and cloud. If you walk a stretch of the Inca road, go with a licensed guide, because the paths are protected and conditions change. The sense of walking where messengers once ran is the real reward.
t.farasfaj@34.5,48.3:
Farasfaj is the kind of place that only makes sense once you have the map open. It sits in the uplands of Hamadan province, in western Iran, on the high farming plateau that the Zagros mountains pile up behind. The nearest real towns are Kangavar to the north-west and Nahavand to the south-east, both a good half hour away, so this is a village stop in open country rather than a place with services. Fill the tank before you leave one of those towns and carry water, because nothing here should be assumed.

The country around is wide and rolling, wheat and orchard land under hills that turn from green to the colour of straw by early summer. Roads across this plateau are generally broad and fast, with long gentle bends and the occasional village that drops you to a crawl for livestock, motorbikes and children. The altitude is well over a thousand metres, which means cool mornings even in summer and hard frost in winter, so spring and early autumn are the seasons I would choose. Afternoon light on the stubble fields is lovely, and the dust that trucks throw up makes it hang in the air like gauze.

What gives the area its weight is the old road running through it. This is the corridor that carried traffic between the Mesopotamian lowlands and the Iranian plateau for thousands of years, passing Hamadan, which was Ecbatana, the capital of the Medes and a summer seat of the Persian kings. Kangavar still has the platform of a large ancient sanctuary that early travellers linked to the goddess Anahita, and further west the cliff of Bisotun carries the great relief and inscription Darius the Great had cut around 520 BC to tell the world how he won his throne. Anyone riding here is on the same line of travel as armies, merchants and pilgrims.

I cannot tell you a specific monument that stands exactly at these coordinates, and I would rather say so than invent one. Treat Farasfaj as a pause in the landscape, a place to look at the mountains, drink tea if someone offers it, and let the scale of the plateau register. If you have a day to spare, put Bisotun on the same ride, and go early, because the cliff face is lit best in the morning and the car park fills by midday.

Be ready for police checkpoints on the main roads, which are routine, polite and usually quick. Keep your documents handy and your speed honest.
t.ur archaeological city@31.0,46.1:
Ur stands on the flat Mesopotamian plain in southern Iraq, close to Nasiriyah, among the oldest cities in the world. Its great ziggurat, a stepped brick platform built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BC, still rises out of the desert, restored and shaped like a huge brick wedding cake with stairs up the front. It was a temple to the moon god Nanna, and the city around it was a major port on what was then the Euphrates, before the river shifted course and the sea retreated. Tradition names Ur as the birthplace of Abraham, which is why Pope Francis held a prayer meeting here in 2021.

The English archaeologist Leonard Woolley dug here in the 1920s and 1930s and found the Royal Cemetery, with tombs full of gold, lapis lazuli and shell inlays, including the famous Standard of Ur and the Queen's lyre, many of which are now in the British Museum and the Iraq Museum. The tombs showed a rich and puzzling culture of ritual burial, with attendants buried alongside their rulers. Nearby, the marshes of southern Iraq, a wetland landscape of reeds and buffalo, have their own World Heritage listing.

The country around is flat, dry and open, with a straight road running out from Nasiriyah through scrub and date palms. There are military and police checkpoints, and permits may be required to enter the site, so it pays to arrange access in advance. The heat in summer is brutal, with temperatures above forty-five degrees and dust in the air, and the best months for a visit are November to March. Sandstorms can reduce visibility to almost nothing.

Nasiriyah is a big city of around four hundred thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and markets, and it is the sensible base. Take a lot of water and a hat, and expect to see the ziggurat in the low sun of early morning, when the brick turns a soft honey colour and the desert is quiet. As elsewhere in the region, check travel advice before planning anything.
t.susa archaeological complex@32.2,48.3:
Susa is among the oldest cities on earth, and one of the most layered. Elamite kings ruled from here from the fourth millennium BC, and later the Persian emperor Darius the Great made it a winter capital of the Achaemenid empire, building a vast palace with a columned hall, the Apadana, with glazed brick friezes of archers and lions. The palace was famous in antiquity, and the Book of Esther in the Bible is set here, in the royal citadel of Shushan. The archaeological mound rises beside the modern town of Shush in Khuzestan, in the hot lowlands at the foot of the Zagros mountains.

French archaeologists dug here from the late nineteenth century, and a castle-like expedition house built by them still crowns the mound. Among their finds was the black stele inscribed with the law code of Hammurabi, carried off as spoils of war by an Elamite king and now in the Louvre, along with the glazed brick friezes. A short walk away is the tomb of Daniel, a white-coned shrine beside the Shavur river that is a place of pilgrimage for Muslims, Jews and Christians. About forty kilometres south-east lies Chogha Zanbil, an Elamite ziggurat that is also on the World Heritage list.

The country is flat, fertile and hot, with irrigated fields of wheat, cotton and sugar cane. The road into Shush from Ahvaz or Dezful is straight and busy with trucks, and speeds are moderate. Summer temperatures often pass forty-five degrees, with a heavy, humid wind, and the only sensible time to visit is the winter half of the year, when days are warm and pleasant. Spring brings green fields and wildflowers.

Shush has some fifty thousand people and has everything you need, including fuel and restaurants serving grilled fish and kebab. Dezful, to the north, is a larger city with a Sassanid bridge. Wear a hat, carry water and walk the mound in the morning, when the light is soft and the brick is warm.
t.kaldar cave@33.6,48.3:
Long before there were gardens, or even farms, people sheltered in the caves of the Zagros. Kaldar Cave lies in the hills near Khorramabad, in the province of Lorestan in western Iran, and it was occupied by Stone Age hunters tens of thousands of years ago. Excavations have found stone tools and the bones of animals that were hunted and eaten here, and the cave is among the important Palaeolithic sites of the region. The entrance faces a valley of oak forest, one of the old forests that once covered the mountains, and the setting is as dramatic as the history.

Lorestan has a long past. The bronze objects of Luristan, finely worked animals, horse fittings and weapons, were made here some three thousand years ago and are found in museums around the world. Khorramabad, the main town, has a castle on a rock called Falak-ol-Aflak, the Heaven of the Heavens, which has Sasanian foundations and was used for centuries, and a good museum in it. The town of a third of a million people has fuel, hotels and restaurants, and makes the obvious base.

The roads around the Zagros are a joy for a rider. They twist through oak and almond woods, over passes and along deep valleys, with sudden views over ridges that fold away to the horizon. The surface is generally good on the main roads and rough on side roads, and trucks are a constant presence. In spring the hills are green, with poppies and tulips in the fields, and the villages smell of woodsmoke and baking bread. Winter brings snow, and the higher roads can be dangerous. Lorestan is also home to nomadic herders who move their flocks to the high pastures in summer.

Vasian, a small place with under two thousand inhabitants, is the closest village, and the cave is not far from the town. Fuel in Khorramabad is straightforward, and the city has many shops. A traditional meal of lamb stew with dried limes, served with fresh bread and herbs, is excellent.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while summer is hot in the valleys. Foreign riders should check the rules for visiting and riding in Iran before they plan.
t.susa@32.2,48.3:
Susa is one of the oldest cities on earth, and the town of Shush in Khuzestan stands on top of it, a low, hot, flat place near the foothills of the Zagros where the Karkheh and Dez rivers water the plain. People have lived here for about six thousand years. It was the capital of the Elamites, and later the winter capital of the Achaemenid Persian kings, and Darius the Great built a vast palace here around 500 BC, with an audience hall whose columns were crowned with bulls. Its workers came from all over the empire, and a famous foundation text records that cedar came from Lebanon, gold from Sardis and ivory from India.

The mound is huge, and at the top of it stands an odd building, a fortress-like castle of brick built by French archaeologists in the 1890s to protect their expedition, in an unlikely mix of Mesopotamian and Gothic styles. The French dug here for decades and carried off treasures to the Louvre, including the Code of Hammurabi, which was found at Susa in 1901 in the form of a black basalt stele, carried off as loot by an Elamite king long before. The museum next to the mound has pottery, seals and sculpture, and a walk around the site shows foundations, brickwork and the outline of Darius's palace.

Nearby is the tomb of the prophet Daniel, a white cone-shaped dome on the riverbank that is a place of pilgrimage for Muslims, Jews and Christians. About forty kilometres to the south-east stands the ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil, another World Heritage Site, built by the Elamite king Untash-Napirisha in the thirteenth century BC.

Riding in Khuzestan is mostly about heat. Summer temperatures can pass fifty degrees, and midday riding is dangerous, so go between November and March, when the air is mild. The roads are flat, straight and often busy with trucks, with long, empty stretches, and in the south the oil industry leaves its mark in flares and pipelines. Shush has about fifty thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and hotels. Try kebab and a glass of dough, the sour yoghurt drink, and the dates that are sold everywhere. Check the foreign-vehicle rules before you plan to bring a bike.
t.ardeshir palace@32.2,48.2:
Across the Shavur river from the great mound of Susa, in the flat farmland of Khuzestan, stand the broken bases of columns that mark one of the later Achaemenid palaces. Ardeshir is the Persian form of Artaxerxes, and the king usually linked with this palace is Artaxerxes II, who ruled for over forty years in the early fourth century BC and left buildings at Susa, Hamadan and Persepolis. The site is also called the Shaur Palace, and in the 1970s excavations by a French team uncovered a columned hall with great stone bases and traces of a pavilion. Little is standing today, so what you see is a field of bases like tree stumps, and you need to bring some imagination.

That is part of its charm, I think. Susa was the winter capital of the Persian kings, who came down from the cold highlands to enjoy the mild season on the lowlands, and the royal court moved between four capitals each year. Here, beside the river, the king could sit in a columned hall open to the breeze and look across to the walls of the old city. The Achaemenids loved water and shade, and Greek writers described the Persian court with a mix of astonishment and disapproval, from the golden plane tree to the gold vine said to stand in the king's chamber.

Today the area around is farmland, with sugarcane, wheat and vegetable plots irrigated from the river, and the town of Shush spills across the plain. The tomb of Daniel, a white conical dome, rises on the bank very close, with an atmosphere of pilgrimage, and the ruins of Susa are a short drive away. For a rider, the roads are flat and straight, with heavy traffic of trucks and pickups, and a lot of dust. The wind in spring can bring sandstorms from the desert.

Plan to visit in winter, between December and February, when temperatures are mild and rain turns the land briefly green. In summer the heat is stupendous and the light is hard and white. Shush itself, only a hundred metres or so away on the map, has fuel, shops and cheap restaurants. Look for a roadside stall selling fresh dates or a glass of sugarcane juice, which is a local drink in the cooler months. Bring water, a hat and some patience for the site's occasional locked gate.
t.yafteh cave@33.5,48.2:
Yafteh Cave is one of the old stones of human history. It lies in the Zagros mountains of Lorestan province, a few kilometres from the city of Khorramabad, in a limestone cliff above the Kashkan river valley. Archaeologists excavated it in the 1960s and found layers of occupation going back tens of thousands of years, with stone tools, bone points and, remarkably, decorated beads and ornaments made from shell and stone, which suggest that people here were making jewellery very early. Together with Kaldar Cave, not far away in the same mountains, it forms part of a prehistoric record of life in the Zagros, a region where people moved between valley floors and mountain pastures with the seasons.

Khorramabad itself is a city of over three hundred thousand people, with a long past. Its landmark is Falak-ol-Aflak, a castle on a rocky hill whose lower levels go back to the Sasanian period and which was rebuilt in the Islamic centuries, and the bridge of Shapur-Khast, a Sasanian structure over the river. The Lurs, who live in this region, have their own language, music and a tradition of nomadic herding, and in spring and autumn you may see families moving with sheep and goats along the road.

The ride is the kind that makes Iran a rider's country. From the Khorramabad area you can follow roads through the Zagros, with mountains cut by gorges, oak woods, steep hairpins and sweeping views. Surfaces vary from smooth to patched, and rockfalls and flocks of animals are possible. Weather is mild in spring, when wildflowers cover the slopes, and hot in summer on the lower slopes, while winter brings snow on the high passes, so check conditions before setting out.

The cave itself is on a hillside, and getting to the entrance involves a short climb on a rough path, so wear proper shoes. Nothing is left in the cave to see except the shape of the rock and the view, but that is enough, standing at the mouth and looking out over the same valley where hunters waited for game. Khorramabad, about fourteen kilometres off, has fuel, restaurants and hotels, and the little town of Vasian has a few shops. A bowl of ash, a thick herb and bean soup, is the local dish to look for.
t.tell eridu archaeological site@30.8,46.0:
Eridu is where the Sumerians said civilisation began. According to their own king lists, kingship came down from heaven and landed first at Eridu, and the city's god, Enki, ruler of the sweet waters beneath the earth, was the keeper of the arts of civilised life. Archaeologists found a sequence of temples stacked one above another, beginning in about 5400 BC, which makes it one of the oldest settlements in Mesopotamia. On top of it all rises the ruined ziggurat of Ur-Nammu, a mud-brick stepped tower built around 2100 BC, now a worn brown stump in the desert.

The site, called Tell Abu Shahrain locally, lies in the far south of Iraq, about thirty-seven kilometres from Nasiriyah and a short drive from Ur. It forms part of the World Heritage listing known as the Ahwar of Southern Iraq, which links the ancient Sumerian cities of Ur, Uruk and Eridu with the marshlands where the Tigris and Euphrates run out into the Gulf. Standing on the ziggurat you look over flat desert, brown and shimmering, with the faint green line of marshes in the distance.

Practically, this is not a casual riding destination. The roads are long and flat, going through desert, with heat that in summer passes forty-five degrees and can reach fifty. Fuel is available in Nasiriyah, a city of around four hundred thousand, and you should carry water and be self-sufficient for the last stretch, which may be a track. Travel in southern Iraq normally requires local guides, permits and up-to-date advice on security, and it is not something to improvise. I do not know the current state of the road to the site, and I would not guess.

If you are lucky enough to visit, go in winter, when days are mild and the sky clear, and the marshes fill with birds. The marsh Arabs, the Ma'dan, still live in reed houses on the water and keep water buffalo, and their way of life has lasted for thousands of years, although it was nearly destroyed in the 1990s when the marshes were drained.

Take shade, silence and a hat, and let the mud-brick tell its story.
t.segment vitkus abra choqetakarpu@-13.1,-:
Manco Inca fled here with his army in 1537, after his great siege of Cusco failed, and Vitcos became the capital of what was left of the Inca Empire. For thirty-five years, in the jungle-covered mountains of Vilcabama, the last independent Incas held out against the Spaniards, raiding Spanish roads, sheltering rebels and keeping alive the old religion. In 1572 the Spaniards finally reached the inner refuge and captured Tupac Amaru, the last Inca, who was taken to Cusco and beheaded in the main square.

The site of Vitcos lies on a hill near the village of Rosaspata, in the valley of Vilcabamba, and nearby stands Yurak Rumi, the White Rock, a huge boulder carved into seats, steps and channels where the Incas held ceremonies. Both are part of the Qhapaq Nan, the Great Inca Road, the web of mountain paths, terraces and stairways that connected the empire from Colombia to Chile and Argentina, and which UNESCO listed in 2014 across six countries. This segment runs from Vitcos towards the Choquetacarpo pass, a high saddle where the trail crosses between valleys.

Getting here is an expedition, not a day-trip. The nearest town of size is Santa Ana, now usually called Quillabamba, a warm, low-altitude town of around twenty-five thousand people, where coffee and cacao are grown. You will find fuel, food and basic repairs there, and little beyond. The road to the Vilcabamba valley is rough, unpaved, steep and exposed, with landslides in the rainy season, river fords and sections where the edge falls away. Only experienced off-road riders with suitable bikes should consider it, and nobody should go alone. The approach from Cusco, over the Abra Malaga pass above four thousand metres, is one of the great high roads of Peru and a fine ride in itself.

Altitude is a serious factor, and nights are cold. The dry season, from May to September, is the safest time, with clear skies. The wet months, from December to March, bring heavy rain and slides.

Take a local guide, because paths are not always signed, and ask permission before crossing farmland. Try the local coffee, which is outstanding.
t.segment machucucho choquecancha@-13.0,-7:
The Urubamba river is the great artery of Inca country, and everything near it feels like a rehearsal for Machu Picchu. This segment of the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road network listed by UNESCO in 2014, runs between two places named Machucucho and Choquecancha in the highlands north-east of Cusco, where side valleys climb from the main river towards high passes and snow peaks. I do not know these two names well enough to place them on a village map, so let me describe the country they belong to rather than invent a spot.

This is the Sacred Valley zone and its neighbours, a region of farmland terraced up steep slopes, with rivers running clear and cold from glaciers. The Incas turned these valleys into their breadbasket, building terraces at every altitude to grow maize, potatoes and other crops at their best elevations, as an agricultural laboratory. Roads connected the terraces to administrative centres and shrines, and many are still used today by farmers and herders. Just beyond the head of the valley are villages with textile traditions, where women weave in natural dyes patterns that have not changed in centuries.

The riding in this part of Peru is memorable. The road from Cusco to Urubamba and Ollantaytambo is paved and scenic, following the river between snowy peaks, with the huge Inca fortress of Ollantaytambo as a highlight. Beyond that, the road over the Abra Malaga pass climbs above four thousand metres, with cloud forest on the far side, a wonderful but cold ride. Side roads to the high valleys are gravel and rock, steep and exposed. Fuel is available in Urubamba, a town of around seven or eight thousand, Cusco and Calca, but not in the hills, so fill up and carry reserve.

Altitude demands respect. Cusco sits at 3,400 metres and most of these roads are higher, so take it easy, drink plenty of water and accept that you will be slow for a day or two. The dry season, from May to September, is best, though mornings are bitterly cold.

Look for the Sunday markets, where you can buy fresh bread, choclo, the huge-kernelled maize, and fresh cheese.
t.te wahipounamu south west new zealand@-4:
South-west New Zealand is the wettest, wildest quarter of the country, and Te Wahipounamu, which in Māori means the place of greenstone, is its official name. The World Heritage area stretches over about two and a half million hectares and takes in four national parks: Fiordland, Mount Aspiring, Aoraki Mount Cook and Westland Tai Poutini. The coordinates here fall deep in Fiordland, west of Te Anau, in country with no through road at all, so what you are being pointed at is a landscape rather than a lay-by.

Fiordland is what happens when glaciers cut into mountains and the sea fills the result. Steep granite walls rise straight out of the water, hung with waterfalls after rain, and the forest clings to rock so thin that after heavy storms whole slopes of trees slide into the fiords in great scars. Rain is the rule. Parts of the district get more than six metres a year, and when it falls the waterfalls multiply into hundreds. When the sun appears, the effect is almost too bright to bear.

For the rider, the nearest real road is the Milford Road, which runs from Te Anau up the Eglinton valley, past Mirror Lakes and the Divide, and through the Homer Tunnel, a 1.2-kilometre bore that passes under the mountains to the Cleddau valley. The road is spectacular and demanding: narrow in places, steep descents on the far side, wet surfaces, and an avalanche risk in winter and spring that can close it without warning. Check conditions before you leave and carry rain gear, a warm layer and a charged phone. Cold air at the tunnel can surprise even in summer.

Fuel matters. Te Anau is the last proper stop for petrol, and Milford has none, so fill up before the long run. Queenstown is a long way back. Sandflies thrive in this country, so insect repellent is as important as anything in your bag, and keas, the mountain parrots, will pick at bike seats and luggage straps if left alone.

Go in a spell of settled weather in summer, start early, and do not expect to complete the day's plan if the rain closes in.
t.cusco@-13.5,-72.0:
Cusco sits at about 3,400 metres in a high Andean valley, and the first thing it asks of you is patience. The air is thin, so even a short walk uphill can leave you breathless, and visitors from sea level often feel it as a headache or a strange tightness for a day or two. Locals will offer you coca tea, which helps a little; rest, water and a light dinner help more. On a motorcycle, thin air also saps engine power, a carburetted bike may run rich and a fuel-injected one will cope better, so do not be surprised if your machine feels a little tired.

This was the capital of the Inca Empire, and the Spanish who took it in 1533 built their city directly on top of the old one. Walk the lanes and you will see Inca stonework, fitted without mortar, used as foundations for colonial churches and houses. The walls survive because they flex in earthquakes, and when quakes hit in 1650 and 1950 the Spanish arches fell while many Inca courses stayed put. Above the city, the huge zigzag walls of Sacsayhuamán look down from the hillside, and if you have time they are worth a visit.

Cusco is the start of the Sacred Valley route, which runs northwest toward Pisac, Urubamba and Ollantaytambo along the Urubamba river, with good tarmac, long curves, farmland and high peaks beyond. Traffic in the city is chaotic, with minibuses, taxis, tuk-tuks and a lot of horn, and the narrow streets of the centre are steep and sometimes stepped. Take it slowly and stay alert, especially after rain, when stone surfaces are polished and treacherous.

Fuel is easy in town, where stations are common on the main avenues, and you should top up before heading out because supplies thin in rural districts. Food is a joy: try roast guinea pig if you are curious, but also quinoa soup, grilled trout and alpaca steaks, followed by a hot chocolate in one of the cafés near the main square.

The dry season, from May to September, offers clear skies and cold nights, while the rainy months of December to March bring green hills and landslides that can block roads.
t.city of cuzco@-13.5,-72.0:
The Incas laid Cuzco out in the shape of a puma, they say, with the fortress of Sacsayhuamán as the head and the Tullumayo stream running along the spine, and while archaeologists argue about how literally to take the story, the city's plan still shows how seriously they took their capital. The name Qosqo means navel in Quechua, a statement of cosmology as much as geography: from here the empire's four quarters, the Tawantinsuyu, spread out in all directions.

At the heart of that world stood the Qorikancha, the Temple of the Sun, whose walls were covered, according to Spanish chroniclers, in sheets of gold. The conquistadors stripped the gold, and the Dominicans built the church and convent of Santo Domingo on the same walls. The result is a curious sight: Baroque cloisters sitting on a base of polished Inca masonry so precise that you cannot slide a blade between the stones. When the 1950 earthquake brought down much of the Spanish building, the Inca foundations barely moved.

For a motorcycle the city is a puzzle. The centre is a maze of steep lanes, one-way streets and cobbles, some of which narrow to a single bike's width, with the added hazards of buses, taxis, wandering dogs and the occasional herd of llamas. Altitude affects riders as well as engines; expect to feel slow at first. Parking near the old centre is tight, so look for a guarded lot and ask your hotel. Rain makes the cobbles greasy, and the dry months between May and September are by far the best.

Fuel is easy to find on the larger avenues that ring the centre, and a city of this size has any spare part or service you are likely to need. Food and coffee are good and cheap; the San Pedro market, a short walk from the plaza, sells fruit juices, bread and local cheese in a big, noisy hall.

Come at dawn if you can, when the stone is still cold, the streets are quiet and the sunlight reaches the high walls of the old town before the crowds do.
t.main square and historic centre@-13.5,-7:
Cusco's main square is built around a simple trick of scale. In Inca times it was a vast open space, called Huacaypata, where armies gathered and ceremonies took place. The Spanish cut it down to the present plaza, lined it with arcades and placed the Cathedral on one side, where it sits on the foundations of an Inca palace. On the opposite flank stands the Jesuit church of La Compañía, whose richly carved facade was designed to outdo the neighbouring cathedral, and legend says the bishop complained to the pope about it.

The plaza is also the site of darker history. In 1781 Túpac Amaru II, the Indigenous leader of a great rebellion against Spanish rule, was executed here after his capture, a moment that still resonates in Peru. Today the square is a gentler place, with balconies full of cafés and restaurants, benches under the trees and children chasing pigeons. The cathedral holds a painting of the Last Supper, in which the Cusqueñan painters gave the table a roasted guinea pig and a local chilli drink, which is the kind of detail locals love to point out.

By bike the centre is more of an arrival than a ride. The streets close to the plaza are narrow, steep and often restricted to pedestrians, and parking is scarce, so leave the motorcycle in a secure garage and walk. Altitude makes uphill strolls tiring, and evenings turn cold quickly, so carry a layer. In the rainy season from December to March, showers come in the afternoon, and stone steps become slippery.

Fuel is available in the lower parts of the city, away from the old core, and cafés and restaurants around the plaza are numerous, if pricey. For something plainer, wander a few blocks up toward San Blas, where artists' workshops and small bakeries cluster along the stepped lanes, and the views back over the red tile roofs are among the best in the city.

Early morning, before the tour groups arrive, is the best time to see the square, and late evening, when it is lit, runs a close second.
t.santiago square and church@-13.5,-72.0:
Santiago, on the south-western side of the historic core, is one of the districts where Cusco feels like a working town rather than a museum. The square and its small church sit among streets lined with shops, workshops and houses that were once on the edge of the Inca city. The Spanish named it after Saint James, their patron in battle, the one who was said to appear on a white horse to help the conquistadors, and the Cusqueños transformed him into a figure linked with thunder and lightning, a good example of how two beliefs merged.

Santiago is not on most itineraries, which is its charm. The streets here are busier and a little scruffier than the postcard centre, with fruit sellers, mechanics and households going about their lives. Nearby, markets sell meat, cheese, herbs and the many varieties of potato that grow in the Andes, and a plate of fresh trout or a bowl of chicken soup in a family eatery costs a fraction of the tourist prices a short walk away.

Riding in this part of the city needs care. The roads are steep, narrow and mostly cobbled or patched, with a stream of minibuses, taxis and trucks mixing with pedestrians. Altitude slows you, so allow extra time, and watch the manholes and gutters, which can be unprotected. Rain makes the stones slick, and on the steepest slopes a small bike can struggle two-up. Try to keep to the main avenues and park in a guarded space overnight.

Fuel is easiest on the broad avenues just outside the old core, and several stations lie a few minutes from the square. Cusco's altitude, around 3,400 metres, means a bike may feel flat, but it should run normally once you are moving. For repairs, small garages are found on the outskirts, and many mechanics are used to working on small and mid-sized motorcycles.

Mornings are best, when the markets are in full swing and the light slants sharply down the narrow streets.
t.almudena and almudena church@-13.5,-72.0:
Almudena lies on the southern edge of Cusco, where the city begins to thin out into the long valley that runs toward Lake Huacarpay and beyond. The church and cemetery there make the area feel more local than touristic: families visit on All Saints' Day in early November, bringing flowers and food, and the whole district seems to slow down into a quiet, respectful day.

The old road southeast out of Cusco is one of the great underrated rides in the region. It follows the Huatanay and then the Vilcanota valleys, past Tipón's Inca terraces and water channels, the huge pre-Inca site of Pikillaqta and the church at Andahuaylillas, whose richly painted interior has earned the nickname of the Sistine Chapel of the Andes. Roads are generally good, with long open stretches and some rough patches, and there are fewer tourists than on the Sacred Valley route.

Riding out from Almudena involves rough city streets at first, with potholes, speed bumps called rompemuelles, and heavy minibus traffic. Be patient; once you clear the outskirts the valley opens, with fields of maize and barley, eucalyptus trees along the roads, and mountains on both sides. Dogs, children and farm animals appear without warning on the verge, and local drivers overtake in ways that visitors might find alarming. Weather in the rainy season, from December to March, can bring landslides and mud, and the afternoon showers are heavy.

Fuel is easier in Cusco than in the valley, so fill the tank before leaving, and bring water and snacks. Small villages along the way offer grilled meat and soup at roadside stalls, and the church at Andahuaylillas is worth the stop for the painted ceiling alone.

Take the road early, when the air is cold and clear, and return before the afternoon cloud builds over the peaks.
t.belen square and church@-13.5,-72.0:
Belén is a small plaza on the south side of Cusco's centre, with a church that dates from the colonial era and a neighbourhood that has long been home to potters and tradespeople. Like much of the city, it was built on Inca land, and the name recalls the hospital and chapel of Bethlehem that the Spanish founded for the care of the sick. The church is modest by Cusco's standards, but its location, away from the busiest tourist streets, gives it an everyday air that many visitors miss.

The street layout here is a good example of the city's ancient grid. Narrow lanes run between high walls of fitted stone, many of which are Inca in origin, and the colonial houses add wooden balconies and tiled roofs on top. Walk even a few minutes and you pass a tiny chapel, a bakery, an open door with a loom or a pottery wheel and a dog asleep in the sun. The locals are friendly and happy to point you toward the next place of interest.

Motorcycles here need patience and light hands. The streets are narrow, steep and cobbled, with uneven stones that shake a laden bike, and wet weather makes them slick. Taxis and minibuses leave little room, and you will often find yourself reversing for oncoming vehicles. Keep your speed down, watch for the steps and gutters at the edge, and park only in a secure place, since theft can be an issue. Altitude takes some energy, so give yourself time at the start of the day.

Fuel is at the stations on the wider avenues to the south and west, a few minutes away. For something to eat, simple restaurants offer lunch menus of soup, a main course and a drink at modest prices, and the nearby streets have many bakeries. If you want to see how Cusco's craftspeople work, a small workshop visit can be arranged through local guides.

Early morning, when the city is quiet and the stones are cool, suits this corner best.
t.central otago vineyard sweep@-44.4,168.5:
The coordinates of this stop fall in roadless alpine country, high in the Southern Alps west of Mount Aspiring, so the honest answer is that the real stop lies in the dry hills of Central Otago a good distance to the east, in the country of schist, vineyards and old gold workings. This is the most southerly wine region in the world, a rain-shadow landscape where the mountains hold off the Tasman Sea weather and leave the valleys cold, bright and dry, with hot days and frosty nights that suit pinot noir.

The vineyards cluster around Gibbston, on the Kawarau river, and Bannockburn, near Cromwell, where tasting rooms stand beside rows of vines on terraces of ancient river gravel. Cromwell has a giant fruit sculpture beside the highway and orchards of cherries, apricots and peaches, which ripen in the summer, and sell at roadside stalls. The gold rush of the 1860s brought thousands of miners to these valleys, and old stone huts, water races and tailings still scar the hillsides. Arrowtown preserves a small Chinese settlement, a reminder of the many Chinese miners who worked the claims. Just up the road from Gibbston, the old Kawarau bridge is where commercial bungy jumping began in 1988.

The riding is superb. The road through the Kawarau Gorge, with its twists above the green river, is a classic, and the roads around Cromwell, Clyde and Alexandra are quiet, with wide views over dry, tawny hills and distant snow. The surface is generally good, but ice can form in the shade in winter, and in summer the heat is intense. The best times are spring, when the blossom is out and the air is clear, and autumn, when the poplars and vines turn gold and red.

The pin is marked for food, and there are good meals to be had at the winery restaurants and the cafés of Cromwell and Arrowtown, using local lamb, cheese and fruit. Fuel is available at Cromwell, Wanaka and Queenstown, so top up before you head into the quieter valleys.

Take your time. Sit on a terrace with a glass of wine, if you are not riding, or a coffee if you are, and watch the light change on the hills. It is a country that looks better the longer you stay.
t.milford road expedition@-45.0,168.0:
The Eglinton Valley is a broad, straight, flat-bottomed trench that a glacier dug through the mountains of Fiordland, and the Milford Road runs down the middle of it. The pin sits on the road here, among red beech forest and golden tussock flats, with the steep grey walls of the Earl Mountains on one side and the Livingstone Mountains on the other. A short walk away, the Mirror Lakes, small ponds beside the road, show a perfect reflection of the peaks on a still morning, and a boardwalk makes it easy to see.

The road to Milford Sound is one of the great drives of New Zealand, and also one of the more demanding. It climbs from Te Anau along the valley, past Lake Gunn and the Divide, and then enters the Homer Tunnel, a rough, unlit tunnel of about 1.2 kilometres blasted through solid granite, which opened in the 1950s after decades of work. At the far end the road drops steeply, in hairpins, to the Cleddau valley and the fiord. Milford is one of the wettest places on Earth, with over six metres of rain a year, and the waterfalls that pour down the cliffs after a downpour are spectacular.

For riders the road is rewarding and sometimes tough. The surface is sealed, with long, gentle curves in the valley and tighter bends at the head, but the weather is the main challenge. Rain, cloud and wind can arrive suddenly, and in winter, snow and avalanche danger can close the road, and chains may be required. Tour buses are common in the middle of the day, so leave early. Kea, the cheeky alpine parrots, gather at the tunnel and may pick at your seat or luggage if left unattended, so keep an eye on them.

Food is also limited, with a small café at Milford and basic facilities at The Divide, so bring snacks. Sandflies are fierce near water, and repellent is a good idea.

Stop at Mirror Lakes if the sky is clear. The reflection of the mountains in still water is a quiet, beautiful sight, and a short walk through the forest helps stretch the back.
t.puerto natales@-51.7,-72.5:
Puerto Natales sits on the edge of the Última Esperanza Sound, the Last Hope, a name given by a sixteenth-century expedition that hoped to find a passage through the channels and found only more water. The town of about twenty thousand people lies on a low shore facing west across the water to the snow-capped peaks of the Patagonian ice field, and the light on a clear evening, with the mountains turning pink, is the best the town has to offer. It was once a base for sheep ranching and meat-packing, and its character is still that of a frontier port.

The reason people come is Torres del Paine, the national park, about a hundred kilometres to the north. On the way there are many things to see. The Cueva del Milodón, twenty-odd kilometres out of town, is a huge cave where the bones and skin of a giant ground sloth were found in the nineteenth century, an animal that went extinct about ten thousand years ago. The writer Bruce Chatwin made it the starting point of his travel book In Patagonia. Beyond that, the road crosses open steppe, with guanaco, rhea and condors, and climbs to the towers of Paine, three granite spires of astonishing steepness.

The riding is open and exposed. The road north is a mix of tarmac and gravel, and the wind is the main problem: Patagonian gusts can reach gale force, sweeping across the steppe and pushing a bike across the lane without warning. It is best in the morning, when the wind is lighter, and the long straight stretches reward a patient rider. Watch for sheep, guanaco and the occasional tourist bus, and expect stones on the gravel stretches.

Puerto Natales has fuel stations, shops and plenty of restaurants, and it is the last place with a full range of services before the park, so fill up and stock up. Try roast lamb cooked over an open fire, the local style, and taste the calafate berry, a sour dark fruit that is turned into jam, liqueur and ice cream. Legend says that if you eat calafate you will return to Patagonia. The best season is November to March, though weather can change in an hour, and cold rain is possible even in midsummer. Carry waterproofs and warm layers whatever the forecast.
t.afzal@32.0,48.9:
Shushtar is a city built on water. On the Karun river in the south-west of Iran, in the province of Khuzestan, it grew up around an ancient system of dams, canals and mills that is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. The engineers of the Sasanian period diverted the river into a long canal, the Gargar, that runs through the city and drives a series of watermills, and then it falls in waterfalls into a lower channel. A great weir, the Band-e Kaisar, was built, according to tradition, by Roman prisoners captured when the Persian king Shapur I defeated the emperor Valerian in the third century.

The town has about 77,000 people, so fuel and food are easy. The old quarter, with its narrow lanes, has houses with cool cellars called sardab, where families once took refuge from the heat. The ruins of the Salasel Castle, a fortress on an island in the river, rise over the old canal, and the mill complex is a maze of tunnels, chambers and stone wheels that you can walk through.

The heat is the main thing to know. In summer, temperatures regularly pass forty-five degrees, and the air is heavy and still, so the best time to ride in Khuzestan is from November to March, when the days are warm and the nights cool. The roads across the plain are flat, straight and fast, with oil pipelines and date palms along the way, and wind-blown dust can reduce visibility. Dezful, a neighbouring city, has its own old bridge and quiet streets.

Further south, the marshes of southern Iraq, home of the Marsh Arabs, form a similar water landscape across the border, and the two regions share a long history. Stay out of the midday sun, drink plenty of water, and let the evening bring you out into the old streets, where the sound of water echoes from the walls.
t.kunji cave@33.4,48.4:
Kunji Cave lies in the foothills of the Zagros mountains, in the province of Lorestan, and it is one of the places where the story of early humans in Iran can be read. The cave, a wide shelter in a limestone cliff, has yielded stone tools and animal bones that show people lived here in the Palaeolithic, tens of thousands of years ago, hunting wild goats and sheep and gathering plants from the oak woods. It is one of several cave sites in the area, which together make Lorestan a key region for the study of prehistory.

The nearest city is Khorramabad, about five kilometres away, with some 330,000 people, and it has fuel, shops and places to eat. The city is dominated by the Falak-ol-Aflak, a castle on a rocky hill, which was probably begun in the Sasanian period and now houses a museum of the region's archaeology, including the famous Lorestan bronzes, small, elegant figures of animals and horse trappings made by the people of this region about three thousand years ago.

Lorestan is the home of the Lur people, who have a long tradition of pastoral life, moving with their flocks between winter and summer pastures. The landscape is one of folded ridges, deep valleys and forests of oak and wild pistachio, and the roads wind through them in long bends with views over river gorges. The Kashkan river runs through the area, crossed by old stone bridges. Surfaces vary, and landslides can follow heavy rain.

Spring is best, when the hills are green and the rivers full, and autumn is pleasant. Winters are cold, with snow at higher altitudes, and summers are hot in the valleys but cool on the heights. Ask for permission before entering the cave, wear sturdy shoes, and bring a torch. The silence inside is old and heavy, and the view from the entrance across the valley is a reward in itself.
t.the iraqi side of huwaizah marshes@31.6,:
The marshes of southern Iraq are one of the oldest inhabited landscapes on earth, and Huwaizah, on the Iranian border east of the Tigris, is the largest of the surviving wetlands. Here the river spreads out into reed beds, open lagoons and channels, and for centuries the Ma'dan, the Marsh Arabs, have lived on floating islands of piled reeds, in houses woven from the same plant. The coordinates sit in the heart of that water world, far from any town.

Their houses, mudhifs, are guest halls built from bundled giant reeds bent into arched ribs, and some stand large enough to have the look of a cathedral. Water buffalo wade through the shallows and are the family's wealth, supplying milk and cream, and the people travel in long, narrow boats called mashoufs, poled through the channels. The way of life continues a tradition that many link to ancient Sumer, whose cities lay at the head of the Gulf not far away.

The marshes were nearly destroyed. In the 1990s, the government of Saddam Hussein drained large areas, building dykes and canals to punish the people who lived there and to remove a refuge for rebels, and most of the wetlands dried to salt crust. After 2003 communities broke the dykes and water returned, and part of the marsh revived. UNESCO listed the Ahwar of Southern Iraq in 2016 as a site of both natural and cultural importance.

Be clear that this is not a casual riding destination. Travel in this region depends on security conditions and permits, roads are limited and there are few services away from towns such as Basra, Amarah or Nasiriyah, and fuel and water need to be arranged well in advance. Heat in summer reaches fifty degrees and the water level varies with drought and upstream dams. Anyone drawn to the story should check official advice and think of it as a place to learn about rather than a route.
t.the ahwar of southern iraq refuge of bio:
Birds are the other half of this story, and the marshes of southern Iraq are a vast and vital place for them. The Ahwar of Southern Iraq, as the World Heritage site is formally called, includes three wetland areas, the Central, Hammar and Huwaizah marshes, and the Refuge of Biodiversity is the part of the listing that acknowledges how much wildlife they hold. The reed beds lie along one of the major bird migration routes between Siberia and Africa, and millions of birds pass or winter here.

Among them are species found almost nowhere else. The Basra reed warbler breeds in the reeds, and the Iraq babbler, a bird of the marsh edge, is known mostly from this country. Pygmy cormorants, pelicans, herons and cranes crowd the lagoons in winter, and the smooth-coated otter, a subspecies of otter that lives in the marshes, hunts the channels. Fish such as the bunni, a large barbel, are an important food, and the waters are shared with turtles, wild boar and jackals on the drier banks.

The landscape is a lacework of reeds, at times standing three or four metres high, with channels and open water that glitters at dawn and dusk. The air carries the smell of wet mud and green stems, and in spring the whole marsh hums with insects and birdsong. t.san jose de maipo@-33.6,-70.4:

t.bourail@-21.6,165.5:
Bourail is the main town of the middle section of New Caledonia's west coast, a cattle town of about 4,800 people that feels more like rural Australia than the Pacific. The Pacific light here is soft in the evening, and the beach at sunset is worth a short detour.
t.lindis pass and tekapo scenic road@-45.0:
Somewhere on the map, thirteen or so kilometres west of the Milford Road, lies a piece of Fiordland National Park with no road of its own. The coordinates fall among the Earl Mountains and the rugged ranges that separate the Eglinton Valley from the deep fiords of the west, a land of steep beech forest, tussock basins, rock walls and tarns, much of it never walked by more than a handful of hunters and trampers in a year. Frost and ice are a real hazard in winter, and chains may be required.

t.queenstown south island@-44.6,169.9:
Omarama sits in the Waitaki basin, a wide, high, dry valley in the lee of the Southern Alps, and the land around it has the stripped look of the South Island's high country, with tawny tussock slopes, braided rivers and a huge sky. The coordinates here fall on the Ahuriri River side of the basin, close to the road that heads toward Lake Benmore, one of the long hydro lakes of the Waitaki system. Omarama is best known to pilots, since the wind that comes over the mountains makes it one of the best gliding sites in the world.

Close to the village, a short side road leads to the Clay Cliffs, a set of eroded gravel and silt pinnacles and ridges, formed by the uplift of old glacial deposits and carved by rain, that look like something from another planet. It is private land and there is a small access fee, a fair price for a surprising walk. The hot afternoon sun on the cliffs gives them a golden colour.

Riding here means big country and big wind. State Highway 8 runs along the valley and crosses the Lindis Pass to the south, with long fast straights and sweeping views over the basin to the Ben Ohau range. The surface is good, the traffic is moderate and the bends are open, but crosswinds can be strong, and temperatures swing from hot to cold in a few hours. On a warm day, the lakes of the Waitaki, with their pale turquoise water coloured by glacial flour, are cold, inviting places for a swim, though the water is mountain cold and cooling.

Omarama has a petrol station, a handful of cafes and a few places to stay, and the Twizel and Otematata townships nearby offer more services. Fuel stops are not frequent in this region, so make use of them. Summer days are long and dry, and winter brings heavy frosts that can leave the shady corners icy, so the best months for this ride are from November to March.
t.lindis pass and tekapo@-44.7,169.8:
The Lindis Pass is the gateway between the Mackenzie country and Central Otago, and the road over it is one of the best known on the South Island. At 971 metres it is the highest point on State Highway 8, a broad saddle of bare, rounded hills covered in snow tussock that glows the colour of old gold in the afternoon sun, and the pass is almost treeless, with the long smooth slopes dropping away on either side into the Lindis Valley. These coordinates sit on the eastern side of that valley, in the sheep station country below the summit, where the road starts its long descent toward Omarama.

There are no towns on the pass itself. The nearest settlement to the south is Tarras, a tiny place with a café, and to the north the village of Omarama. For food, that means planning, and for fuel it means filling the tank before you leave Wanaka or Cromwell, or topping up at Omarama. Plenty of riders have run low out here, and the next station can feel very far away when the needle starts to drop.

The riding is a pleasure. The road climbs gradually through open country with wide, flowing bends and broad views, and on the descent it opens into long, fast sweeps beside the Lindis River. The surface is good, though snow and ice can close the pass for a few hours in winter, and frost lingers on the shady corners until late morning. Weather changes fast. The wind can be powerful and gusty, and a sunny afternoon can turn to sleet in an hour.

The pass was a Māori route long before European settlers, a way to carry greenstone and food across the ranges, and in the 1860s gold prospectors and sheep farmers used it too. Some of the old runs are still working stations. Pull off at the lookout near the top and take a moment to listen to the wind in the tussock. In autumn, from April to May, the colours are at their best and the traffic is lighter.
t.haast@-43.9,169.0:
Haast is the last outpost before the wilderness. The pin lands in the small settlement at the mouth of the Haast river, in the far south-west of the South Island of New Zealand, where about two hundred and fifty people live between the Tasman Sea and the Southern Alps. For decades, it was cut off by rivers and forest, and the road north to Fox Glacier was only completed in 1965, making it the last link in the West Coast highway.

The road from here, State Highway 6, runs in two directions, both superb. North, it follows the coast through rainforest, past lakes, beaches and viewpoints such as Knights Point, to Fox and Franz Josef glaciers, where the ice descends almost to the rainforest. East, it climbs through the valley of the Haast river to the Haast Pass, at 563 metres, a low crossing of the Alps, then drops to Makarora and the lakes of Wanaka and Hawea. The bends are long and flowing, the surface is good, and the scenery is among the finest in the world, with waterfalls, beech forest and mountains. Rain is heavy, up to several metres a year, so waterproofs are essential. Drive on the left, and watch for one-lane bridges.

The area is wild and wet. Mount Aspiring National Park lies inland, and the coast is part of the Te Wāhipounamu world heritage area. Sandflies are infamous, and a good repellent is worth buying. The beaches are littered with driftwood, and the air smells of salt and bush. Haast has a small museum, a few cafes and a visitor centre.

Fuel is available in Haast, but it is the only reliable place for many kilometres, so fill your tank, since the next stations are far to the north and east. Carry food for the road, as villages are small and cafes may close early.

Let the rain pass if it comes, and watch the clouds shift on the peaks. The mountains reveal themselves slowly.
t.milford road@-44.9,168.9:
This stretch of road is the Crown Range, and if the ride is called the Milford Road, it is because this is the way you leave Queenstown's orbit and swing back toward the lakes. It is the highest paved main road in New Zealand, topping out at around 1,076 metres, linking the Wakatipu basin to Cardrona and Wanaka by a route that looks improbable on a map and feels even more improbable once you are on it.

Higher up, the landscape strips back to tussock, bare schist and long views over the Wakatipu basin, with the Remarkables standing stern across the valley. Weather changes fast. I have been warm in Arrowtown and been in sleet at the summit forty minutes later, and in winter there can be snow and ice, with chains advised or required on occasion. Check conditions before setting off.

Arrowtown, ten kilometres away, is worth knowing about for its own sake. It began as a gold town in the 1860s when prospectors worked the Arrow River, and the Chinese miners who arrived afterwards left behind a restored settlement of small stone and sod huts beside the river. Autumn here is exceptional, when the poplars and willows turn gold along the main street and the hills behind turn to rust. It is a good place for a pie, a flat white and a rest before the climb, and there is fuel in town.

Queenstown, twenty-five kilometres off, has everything a rider could want in the way of fuel, food and beds, but also summer crowds that fill the roads. Over the top, Cardrona has a famously photogenic pub, a hotel dating from the 1860s gold rush, set in a nearly empty valley with a ski field above it. Wanaka, a bit further, sits on its own lake and is gentler and quieter than its flashier neighbour.

The best light comes in the evening, when low sun rakes across the basin and the schist glows. Take it slowly on the descent toward Arrowtown, because the bends tighten, and watch out for the cyclists who like this climb as much as the riders do.
t.glenorchy lake road@-45.0,169.1:
Lake Dunstan lies in the heart of Central Otago, a long, narrow reservoir formed when the Clyde Dam was built, and the district around it, Cromwell, Bannockburn and the Pisa Range, has a dry, sunny climate that is unusual in New Zealand. The coordinates here lie on the western shore, a few kilometres from Cromwell, in a land of schist hills and stony paddocks, with the Pisa Range rising to the west. Cromwell itself is a town of about five thousand people, a place of orchards and vineyards that calls itself the fruit bowl of the south, and it is marked by a giant fruit sculpture at the entrance.

The Kawarau Gorge to the west, on the road to Queenstown, is the site of the first commercial bungy jump, at the Kawarau Bridge in 1988, so if you want to throw yourself off something, it is on the way.

The road between Cromwell and Queenstown through the Kawarau Gorge is a winding, fast and scenic route along the river, with tight bends, rock walls and the turquoise water below. The Crown Range road, climbing from Arrowtown over a high saddle with hairpins at the top, is the other route, and it is the highest main road in New Zealand. In summer it is hot and dry, in winter it can be icy and snow-covered, with chains needed. Watch your speed in the gorge, since police radar is common.

Fuel is straightforward in Cromwell, and there are cafes and bakeries in the old town, which was partly flooded by the dam. The wineries around Bannockburn produce pinot noir that is worth a taste, though the rider will have to settle for a bottle in the pannier. Autumn, when the poplars along the river turn gold and the sky is clear, is the best time of year for riding in Central Otago.
t.glenorchy@-45.0,169.1:
The coordinates here do not sit at Glenorchy at the head of the lake, but on the other side of the Wakatipu basin where the roads meet the Kawarau River, in the country around Gibbston. t.haast pass west coast@-44.4,169.2:
This is the stretch of State Highway 6 north of Wanaka, where the road runs along the shore of Lake Wanaka and then crosses the narrow Neck between Wanaka and Lake Hāwea, before heading north into the Haast Pass country. The summit at 563 metres is low for an Alpine pass, which is why it was chosen as a route, and the highway was only completed in the 1960s. Before that, Māori used the pass to carry greenstone, and European explorers made their way through in the 1860s. Along the road there are waterfalls, short walks and bridges over blue-green rivers, including the Blue Pools near Makarora, where trout hang in the clear water and brave swimmers take a plunge in the icy pool.

The road starts with open lakeside bends, then runs through the Makarora valley with beech forest on both sides, then climbs steadily to the pass, and finally descends to the coast with long, flowing bends through rainforest.
