t.eglinton valley@-45.0,168.0:
The Eglinton Valley is a long, flat-floored glacial trough in the heart of Fiordland, and the Milford Road runs straight down the middle of it for kilometres. The valley is walled by steep mountains, covered at their feet in red and silver beech forest and, higher, in bare grey rock, and the valley floor itself is a mosaic of golden tussock flats, meandering streams and clear pools. The effect is wide, quiet and impressive, and the road seems to disappear into the distance between the peaks.

There are a handful of stops that are worth the time. The Mirror Lakes, a short walk from the road, reflect the mountains in still water on a calm day, and a boardwalk makes the visit easy. Lake Gunn, further along, is a beech-lined lake with a short nature walk, and the camping grounds beside the road, simple and cheap, are popular with those who want to wake up in the valley. At Knobs Flat the valley opens into broad meadows where deer graze at dusk.

For a rider, the Eglinton is a pleasure. After the long, fast approach from Te Anau, the road is flat and smooth, with only a few gentle bends, and it gives you time to look around. The corners begin at the head of the valley, where the road climbs toward The Divide and the road to Homer Tunnel. Traffic is steady, with coaches and camper vans, and frost and ice can linger in the shade, so be careful on cold mornings. The weather turns quickly, and you can ride from sunshine into rain within minutes.

Food is scarce, so bring a lunch and a flask. The kea, the cheeky alpine parrot, is common at the road's end, and will pull at your luggage if you give it a chance. Sandflies are fierce around the lakes, so carry repellent. In the early morning, mist hangs in the valley and the first light turns the tussock gold.
t.homer tunnel@-44.8,168.0:
Homer Tunnel is one of the great curiosities of New Zealand roads: a rough, unlined bore through a wall of granite, about 1.2 kilometres long, that connects the Hollyford and Cleddau valleys and opens the way to Milford Sound. Work began in 1935, when men with picks and shovels were hired to dig it as a Depression relief project, and it took until 1954 to finish, since avalanches, floods and the Second World War delayed progress. The tunnel's mouth sits at about 945 metres, at the foot of a vast cirque of rock walls and waterfalls, and the Homer Saddle above it was named after the man who found it in 1889.

Riding through is a strange and thrilling business. The tunnel is dark and damp, with bare rock walls and water dripping from the ceiling, and its floor slopes downhill at about one in ten toward the Milford side. Traffic is controlled by lights, so you may wait some minutes at the entrance, which is a good chance to look at the cliffs and listen to the sound of water. Take your sunglasses off before entering, and be careful of the wet surface, especially in winter, when ice builds up on the road.

After the tunnel, the road descends to Milford Sound in a series of tight hairpins, with spectacular views down the Cleddau valley. The descent is steep and winding, with tight bends, and the surface is usually good but wet. Avalanches are a real risk in winter and spring, and the road can be closed at short notice, so check the road status before setting out. Chains may be required between May and November.

The kea parrots gather at the tunnel entrance and are excellent at stealing food and tearing rubber, so do not leave your gloves on the seat. Take a flask and some food, as Milford itself has only a small cafe. The scenery is magnificent in any weather, and when the rain falls, hundreds of waterfalls spring from the cliffs.
t.ollantaytambo@-13.3,-72.3:
Ollantaytambo is an Inca town in the Sacred Valley of Peru, about 2,800 metres above sea level, and unlike most Inca sites it is not a ruin: people live here in houses laid out on the original Inca street plan, and the streets, with their stone channels of running water, are some of the oldest continuously inhabited in South America. Above the town, a huge stepped terrace climbs the mountainside to a temple complex, built for the emperor Pachacuti in the fifteenth century, with enormous stones fitted so tightly that a knife blade will not pass between them.

The stones are the astonishing part. The great red granite blocks of the Temple of the Sun were quarried on the opposite side of the valley, several kilometres away, and moved across the Urubamba River and up the slope, a task that still baffles engineers. Ollantaytambo was also the site of one of the few Inca victories over the Spanish. In 1536 Manco Inca flooded the plain below the fortress and rained stones and arrows on the cavalry of Hernando Pizarro, who was forced to retreat, though the Incas later withdrew to the jungle.

For a rider, the road along the Sacred Valley from Cusco through Urubamba is a pleasure, with a smooth, well-surfaced highway that follows the river between snow-capped peaks and terraced fields. The bends are open, the traffic is busy with buses and trucks, and the villages have speed bumps, so stay alert. The air is thin, and the sun is strong, with a cold wind from the mountains. Mototaxis and dogs are everywhere, and the cobbled streets of the town are best explored on foot.

Ollantaytambo is also the station for the trains to Machu Picchu, since no road reaches that site, and the town fills with travellers in the morning. Fuel is available in Urubamba, about seventeen kilometres to the south-east, so fill the tank there. The town has plenty of cafes, bakeries and small restaurants, and the Peruvian speciality of choclo, giant-kernelled corn, with cheese, is a good simple lunch. Evenings are cold, and the stars are exceptionally bright.
t.baie saint paul@47.4,-70.5:

The town has long been an artists' town. The painters of the Group of Seven, including A. Y. Jackson, came here in the early twentieth century to paint the folded hills and the old farms, and the galleries on the main street, rue Saint-Jean-Baptiste, carry on the tradition, with studios, craft shops and cafes in old wooden houses. It was also the birthplace of the Cirque du Soleil, which grew from a troupe of street performers working in the town in the early 1980s.

There is a strange fact under the landscape. The whole region of Charlevoix lies inside the remains of a huge meteorite crater, nearly fifty-five kilometres across, formed some four hundred million years ago, and the odd, tumbled terrain of hills and valleys is partly the result. The area is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, protecting forests, tidal marshes and farmland.

The stretch from Baie-Saint-Paul toward La Malbaie is among the most celebrated in Quebec, with gradients of ten per cent in places, bends that tighten, and farms and villages on every ledge. The surface is generally good. Traffic on weekends and in the foliage season, from late September to mid-October, can be heavy, with tour buses and cars, so a weekday morning is best.

Charlevoix is also a food region, with a marked route of farms, bakeries and cheese makers. The local cheeses, made from cow's milk, are among the best in the province, and the lamb that grazes on the salt marshes is a regional specialty. The town has fuel stations, supermarkets and a good choice of restaurants and cafes, and Saint-Jean-Port-Joli, to the southwest across the river, is the next large place. Summer evenings are mild and long, and fog sometimes drifts up from the river in the morning. Winter is long and cold, and the roads can be icy.
t.la malbaie@47.7,-70.2:
La Malbaie is where the summer people used to come. The town of nine thousand lies at the mouth of the Malbaie river on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, about a hundred and fifty kilometres downstream from Quebec City, where the river widens and turns salty, and it has been a resort since the nineteenth century, when wealthy Canadians and Americans began to build summer houses along the shore at Pointe-au-Pic. William Howard Taft, later president of the United States, was one of them, and spent his summers here for many years. The Manoir Richelieu, a grand turreted hotel that overlooks the river, was built in the early twentieth century and still dominates the skyline.

The name means bad bay in French, and it is said to have been given by Samuel de Champlain in 1608 after his ship ran aground on a sandbar at the mouth of the river. Whatever the truth, the bay today is a pleasant place, with a promenade, restaurants, and views across the river to the south shore, nearly twenty kilometres away, visible as a blue line on clear days. The tides rise and fall noticeably, as the river here is still an estuary.

The riding in Charlevoix is some of the best in eastern Canada. Route 138 follows the shore, rising over headlands and dropping to river mouths with steep gradients and curves, with the farmland spread over the slopes and the village churches standing at the water. Surfaces are good, though frost heaves can damage them in spring. Inland, the Malbaie river runs through a deep glacial valley in the Hautes-Gorges national park, where cliffs rise nearly eight hundred metres, but the park is reached by a long, partly unpaved road, so check conditions.

East of La Malbaie, the road continues to Saint-Siméon, where a ferry crosses the river to Rivière-du-Loup, an hour or so on the water, and a good way to make a loop of the trip. Check the schedule and reserve for a motorcycle in summer, since the crossings fill. La Malbaie has fuel stations, supermarkets and a full range of services, and the stretch beyond has fewer, so fill the tank. Late June to October is the best time, though the autumn colours in late September are famous and draw crowds. On a clear evening, the light on the river is gold and rose.
t.levis@46.8,-71.2:

t.abancay@-13.6,-72.9:

Fog and rain can move in quickly, particularly in the wet season from December to March, and at times, the road is blocked by rockfalls. The dry months, from May to October, are the best period for riding.

Abancay has fuel, workshops, shops, restaurants and a good range of hotels, so it is an easy place to rest and prepare. Curahuasi, a village on the way from Cusco, is known for its anise, which is grown in the valley and sold in markets across Peru, and the sweet, liquorice scent of the harvest drifts across the fields. In the city, you can find hearty stews, grilled guinea pig and a dessert of fried dough with honey. After the climb and the descent, a meal and a rest are well earned.

The surrounding country is a land of canyons, with warm, dry valleys planted with sugar cane and avocados and high, cold plateaus above. The region is famous among walkers for Choquequirao, an Inca site on a ridge above the canyon, reached by a long and difficult trek rather than by road. Condors are common in the thermals above the gorge, and the changing light on the mountains gives the whole area a richness of colour. It is a stage on a long road, but an interesting one.
t.puquio@-14.7,-74.1:
Puquio is a small highland town at around 3,200 metres in the Lucanas province, high above the coastal desert, and it stands at the end of one of the most dramatic climbs in Peru. The road from Nazca begins almost at sea level in a hot, dry desert and rises in the space of a few hours to the cold, windy plateau of the Andes, with vast, empty slopes, deep gorges and sudden changes of temperature. Puquio is where the climb pauses, a town of about ten thousand people with a big plaza, a market and a church, set in a bowl of hills.

The ride up is a challenge and a delight. The road leaves the Pan-American Highway and climbs through desert hills, then onto a high plateau of tawny grass. The surface is mostly paved, with some rough patches and landslides, and the bends are long and sweeping in places. Fog is common near the top, and temperatures fall quickly, so a jacket for the cold is as essential as a thin shirt at the bottom. Part of the route crosses the Pampa Galeras reserve, a huge expanse of grassland where vicuñas graze in large numbers, and you may see herds from the road.

The climb is hard on engines as well as riders, with power loss at height, and the long descents wear brakes, so check your equipment before you set out. Puquio has fuel, simple hotels and restaurants serving soups, roast meat and potatoes, which are welcome after the cold. Take time to adjust to the altitude, since the change from the coast can bring headaches and breathlessness. Drink water and avoid heavy meals on arrival.

Puquio is known in Peru for its traditions, particularly the scissor dance, in which dancers perform athletic feats to the music of harp and violin in a tradition that mixes Andean ritual and Spanish colonial influence. The town has also long been a stopping point on the route between the coast and the highlands, and its position among the high pastures gives it a rural, unhurried feel. The sky at night is dense with stars. Wrap up warmly, watch the light fade over the hills, and enjoy the thin, clear air.
t.ayacucho@-13.2,-74.2:
Ayacucho is one of the great colonial cities of the Andes, a town of about 140,000 people in a high, dry valley at around 2,750 metres, and it has a reputation for churches, crafts and Holy Week processions. The Quechua name is often translated as corner of the dead, and the history of the region is, in some respects, rooted in conflict. In 1824, the Battle of Ayacucho, fought on a high plain nearby, ended Spanish rule in South America, and the region later suffered badly during the internal conflict of the 1980s and 1990s. Today, the city has recovered its calm, and the old centre is a pleasure to walk around.

For a rider, Ayacucho is a major stop on the road between Cusco and Lima. It has fuel, workshops, supermarkets, banks, restaurants and a wide range of hotels, and it is a good place to rest, fill up and repair. The plaza, with its arcades and cathedral, is lively in the evening, and the many small churches, said to number in the dozens, are beautiful. Traffic can be heavy and the streets steep, so ride carefully. Try the puca picante, a stew of potatoes and pork in a peanut and chilli sauce, and a sweet pastry from the market.

The surrounding country is a land of high valleys and steep roads. The road toward Huancavelica climbs out of the Ayacucho basin and across high, cold plateaus, with views over a patchwork of fields and dark ridges. The surface is mostly paved, with occasional damage, and bends are frequent. Fog, hail and rain can come at any time, especially from December to March, and nights are cold. From May to October, the weather is drier and the light is brilliant.

Nearby, the ruins of Wari, the capital of an empire that preceded the Incas by centuries, spread across a dry hillside, and the village of Quinua, famous for its ceramics, stands close to the battlefield. Easter is the great time in Ayacucho, with processions, flower carpets and a week of music and food that draws visitors from all over Peru. If you pass through at other times, the quiet streets and the smell of woodsmoke and baking bread still give a sense of a city that is proud of its past.
t.huancavelica@-12.8,-75.0:
Huancavelica is a high, cold city of about forty thousand people, standing at nearly 3,700 metres in the central Andes, and its fortune was built on a metal that is now regarded as a poison. Under the Spanish, the nearby mine at Santa Bárbara produced mercury, which was used to extract silver from the ore of Potosí, and for centuries it was one of the most important mines in the colonial world. The conditions for the miners, many of them forced labourers, were appalling. Today the city is quiet, with a handsome plaza, a cathedral and a collection of colonial churches built in the time of that wealth.

The road from Ayacucho is a high, lonely ride across the puna, the cold grassland of the Andean plateau, with a few villages, herds of llamas and alpacas, and far-off snow peaks. The surface is mostly paved, with some rough sections, and the bends are long. At this height, the air is thin and the weather can change rapidly, with sun, hail and sleet in the same hour, and nights below freezing for much of the year. The best months are May to September, when the skies are clear, though even then you need warm gloves and layers.

Huancavelica has fuel, shops, simple restaurants and guesthouses, and it is a good place to stock up before the next high pass. Food is hearty and simple, with soups, potatoes and roast meat, plus warming drinks such as muña tea, which is brewed from an Andean mint and is thought to help with altitude. The city is also the end of a famous narrow-gauge railway from Huancayo, a slow train that climbs through spectacular country.

The surrounding villages are known for their textiles and for festivals that mix Catholic and Andean traditions, and the region has one of the richest folk cultures in Peru. There are hot springs close to the city, and the high lakes are home to flamingos and Andean geese. The smell of wood smoke hangs in the cold air, and the stars at night are bright and close. It is a remote, rugged place with a history that rewards a little study, and it is an honest introduction to the high Andes.
t.vinicunca@-13.9,-71.3:
Nobody paid much attention to this ridge until the snow started thinning a few years back and the stripes underneath showed up. Vinicunca, the so-called Rainbow Mountain, sits in the Vilcanota range south-east of Cusco, and the colours are plain geology: layers of sediment stained by different minerals, tilted and then exposed, rust-red where iron has oxidised, mustard and cream where other salts and sandstones sit. The summit viewpoint is a little over 5,000 metres, which puts it in the same air as the highest passes in the Alps with another kilometre on top.

The ride there is the best part, honestly, and it is a slow one. You leave Cusco on the valley road toward Sicuani, pass through the small Quechua towns along the Vilcanota river, with Checacupe and Qquea among the names on the signs, and then turn up into the hills on a road that gets narrower, rougher and colder with every climb. Expect fields of potatoes and quinoa, stone walls, llamas and alpacas on the verges, women in layered skirts and bowler hats flagging down the occasional minibus. Surface changes without warning, so keep your speed honest, and give the weather its due: afternoons bring hail and cloud, mornings are clear and bitterly cold.

Be clear about what the gate means. The last stretch to the viewpoint is a walking trail, and a steep one at this height, with horses for hire in the high villages if your lungs say no. The bike stays parked, so go early, because the crowds that arrive by tour bus from Cusco in the small hours are real and the light is flat by midday. Spend a couple of nights in Cusco first to acclimatise, drink coca tea if it appeals, and do not be proud about slowing down.

For fuel, do not count on the villages up here. The towns nearby are only a few thousand people each and are not somewhere I would bet on a pump, so fill the tank in Cusco, or at Sicuani if you are coming from the south, and carry nothing you do not need. Bring a warm layer and rain gear whatever the sky looks like at breakfast. The reward is a ridge that looks painted, a view across a valley of glaciated peaks, and the particular silence of thin air.
t.segment portada rumiqolqa ch uspitacana@:
South-east of Cusco, the Vilcanota valley narrows at a place called Rumicolca, and a massive stone gateway stands across the old road. Built originally by the Wari, the empire that preceded the Inca, as part of an aqueduct, and later converted by the Inca into a controlled entrance to the Cusco valley, the gateway of Rumicolca marked the checkpoint where travellers and goods were inspected. The segment of the Qhapaq Ñan between Rumicolca and Chuspitacana is part of the Andean road system inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2014, and its stones still carry the marks of the people who walked it.

Nearby, Pikillaqta, a Wari city of the first millennium AD, spreads over a hillside, with hundreds of buildings in a rigid grid, an impressive sight. The village of Andahuaylillas, a few kilometres away, has a church with richly painted walls and ceilings, one of the finest colonial interiors in Peru.

Oropesa, ten kilometres away, is famous for its bread, baked in wood-fired ovens and sold along the road in large round loaves, and Urcos, also about ten kilometres away, is a market town with fuel and basic services. The landscape is high and dramatic, at over 3,000 metres, with the river flowing between mountains, fields of corn and potatoes, and eucalyptus trees.

Riding in the Andes is challenging and rewarding. The main road from Cusco to Puno and Lake Titicaca runs through this valley, and it is paved and busy with buses and trucks. Side roads are often unpaved and steep. Altitude affects riders and machines, so take time to acclimatise in Cusco before riding, drink plenty of water, and avoid heavy meals. Weather changes quickly, with sun, rain, hail and cold in a single day. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time to ride. Try cuy, roast guinea pig, chicharrón and chicha morada, a purple corn drink.
t.segment cusipata santa cruz de occobamba:
South of Cusco, the Vilcanota River runs through a broad, fertile valley flanked by high mountains, and along it ran one of the most important stretches of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that linked an empire stretching from Ecuador to Chile. The route from Cusco to Lake Titicaca followed this valley, and sections of the original road, some paved with stone, some cut into the hillside, still survive. The segment between Cusipata and Santa Cruz de Occobamba went onto the World Heritage list in 2014 as one strand of the Qhapaq Ñan.

The towns along the valley tell the story of the conquest. Checacupe, about nine kilometres away, has an old Inca bridge site and colonial bridges side by side, as well as a modest-looking adobe church with an astonishingly rich interior of gilded altars and murals. Further south, Raqchi has the remains of a huge Inca temple dedicated to Viracocha, with a central adobe wall that still stands over ten metres high. Combapata, Tinta and Sicuani are market towns with lively Sunday markets, where you can see people in traditional dress selling potatoes, quinoa and woven textiles.

The altitude here is around 3,400 metres, which means thin air, cold nights and strong sun. Altitude sickness is a real risk for anyone arriving from the coast; spend a few days acclimatising in Cusco before riding, drink lots of water and coca tea, and do not underestimate the effects. Engines lose power too. The valley is also a gateway to Vinicunca, the so-called Rainbow Mountain, reached from Pitumarca, close to Checacupe; the striped mountain rises to over five thousand metres and is hugely popular.

The road along the valley is the main highway from Cusco to Puno, well paved and relatively easy, but shared with fast buses and trucks. Watch for animals on the road, especially llamas, sheep and dogs, as well as speed bumps through villages. Urcos, the nearest larger town, and Checacupe both have fuel and simple food, though quality varies; fill up wherever you can. Try a bowl of chairo soup or trout from the rivers, and be ready for sudden rain or hail in the wet season, from December to March.
t.segment plaza inca hanan hauk aypataqoll:
Every road of the Inca empire began here. The great square of Cusco, which the Incas called Hauk'aypata, was the ceremonial heart of Tawantinsuyu, the land of the four quarters, and from it the main roads radiated out to the four parts of the empire, to Quito in the north, to Chile and Argentina in the south, to the jungle in the east and the coast in the west. The square was much larger than today's Plaza de Armas and was covered, according to the chroniclers, with sand brought from the coast, in which offerings of gold and silver were buried. Here, mummies of past rulers were brought out for festivals, and the Inca received ambassadors and celebrated victories.

The Spanish built their own city right on top of the Inca one, and Cusco is one of the most striking examples of that layering. The cathedral stands on the site of an Inca palace, the Jesuit church on another, and the walls of colonial houses rest on Inca foundations of perfectly fitted stones, some with a dozen angles. The Qorikancha, the temple of the sun, was turned into the convent of Santo Domingo, and its Inca stonework survives inside. Cusco and its historic centre, along with the Qhapaq Ñan, are World Heritage sites.

Riding into Cusco takes nerves: steep, narrow streets, many of them cobbled, sometimes one-way, often crowded with taxis, pedestrians and tourists. The city is at around three thousand four hundred metres, and newcomers should allow a few days to acclimatise before riding hard. The real treat is out of town. The road north over the hills to Pisac drops into the Sacred Valley of the Urubamba in a long series of bends with spectacular views, and from there you can follow the valley to Ollantaytambo or climb to the salt pans of Maras and the circular terraces of Moray. Further afield, the road towards Abancay and the passes beyond are among the great roads of South America.

Fuel, mechanics and accommodation are easily available in Cusco. The food scene is excellent, from street stalls to upscale restaurants: try a bowl of quinoa soup, alpaca, or, if you are adventurous, cuy, the roast guinea pig. Coca tea helps with the altitude, and the chicha, maize beer, sold in houses marked by a red flag, is a local tradition.
t.the central marshes@31.1,47.1:
Between the Tigris and the Euphrates, in the far south of Iraq, lies a world of water, reeds and sky: the Mesopotamian Marshes, home for thousands of years to the Ma'dan, the Marsh Arabs, who build houses and great arched guest halls, the mudhif, entirely from reeds, travel by narrow boats called mashoof and keep herds of water buffalo. The Central Marshes are one of the main areas of this wetland, listed in 2016 with the archaeological cities of Ur, Uruk and Eridu as the Ahwar of Southern Iraq, a World Heritage Site that joins nature and the earliest cities of Sumer.

The marshes were almost destroyed in the 1990s, when the regime of Saddam Hussein drained them with canals and dykes, partly to punish the people who lived there, and most of the Ma'dan were forced out. After 2003, local people broke the dykes and water returned to large areas, though drought, upstream dams and falling river flows now threaten the marshes again. In wet years the reed beds teem with birds, fish and buffalo; in dry years, much of the water vanishes.

Chibayish, on the edge of the Central Marshes, is the main base for visits, and local boatmen take visitors out through the channels to see reed villages, buffalo and birds. The light at dawn and dusk, when mist lies on the water and the reeds glow gold, is unforgettable.

Getting here involves long, flat, hot roads across the alluvial plain from Nasiriyah or Basra, with checkpoints, trucks and the occasional sandstorm. Summer temperatures often pass fifty degrees, making midday travel dangerous; winter is mild and the best time to visit.

Travel in Iraq requires careful planning: many governments advise against travel to parts of the country, and visas, permits and security arrangements can change. Fuel is cheap and available in the towns, including Al-Fuhud, thirty four kilometres away, and Nasiriyah. Try masgouf, carp split and grilled beside an open fire, and the buffalo milk cream, geymar, eaten with bread and date syrup for breakfast.
Choquequirao is sometimes called the sister of Machu Picchu, and you can tell why when you see the photographs: a ridge of white-walled terraces and plazas, perched above a canyon, with snow peaks looming in the background. It is also a good deal harder to reach. The ruins sit at around three thousand metres on the far side of the Apurímac valley, a day's hard walk from the end of the road, and a fraction of the visitors who crowd Machu Picchu make the journey. The name is usually translated as cradle of gold.

The path you follow is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that UNESCO listed in 2014, and the segments around Choquequirao include sections with original paving and stairs that drop into the canyon and climb out again. Nearby, the town of Abancay, the capital of the Apurímac region, is the practical base. The Apurímac river below is fast and deep, and its name is generally given as the great speaker, a nod to the roar of the water in the canyon. The valley is home to condors, which ride the thermals on the cliffs.

On the road, the stretch between Abancay and Cusco is a long, winding highway, mostly paved, that crosses high passes and drops into deep valleys, with lots of bends, trucks and occasional rockfall. Curahuasi, on the way, is known for its anise, and the Saywite stone, a huge carved boulder from the Inca period, lies near the road. The turn-off toward Cachora, the usual starting point for the trek to Choquequirao, is rougher and narrower, with exposed edges and landslide patches in the rainy season, which runs roughly from December to March.

Abancay, about thirty kilometres away, is a town of fifty thousand or so, with fuel, shops and cheap restaurants. The road to Cachora has nothing, so fill up in Abancay and carry water and food. The ruins themselves are reached on foot or by mule, and the trek is usually done in four days with a guide, so leave the bike somewhere safe and plan for cold evenings.
t.the west hammar marshes@30.8,46.7:
The marshes of southern Iraq lie where the Tigris and Euphrates come together on their way to the Gulf, a vast network of reed beds, lagoons and channels that was, until recent decades, home to one of the oldest ways of life on earth. The West Hammar Marshes are the westernmost, south of the city of Nasiriyah, and this stop lies about fifteen kilometres from the small town of Al Fuhud. UNESCO inscribed the Ahwar of Southern Iraq in 2016, along with the ancient Sumerian cities of Ur, Uruk and Eridu, which stood on the edge of this same wetland.

The Marsh Arabs, or Ma'dan, have lived here for thousands of years, building houses and guesthouses of woven reeds with arched roofs, moving about in long, narrow boats poled through the channels, and raising water buffalo. In the early 1990s, the government of Saddam Hussein drained most of the marshes, partly to punish people who had sheltered rebels and partly to open the land, and the wetland shrank to a fraction of its size. After 2003, local people broke the dams and the water returned, and much of the marsh has recovered, though droughts and upstream dams on the rivers still threaten it. It is an extraordinarily important place for birds, with millions of migrating waterfowl in winter, as well as the endangered Basra reed warbler, and there is a distinct smell of water, mud and reeds.

I should be honest that this is not a typical ride. Travel in southern Iraq needs careful planning, with advice about security, permits and checkpoints, and most visitors travel with a local guide. The main road from Basra to Nasiriyah crosses flat desert and farmland with heavy truck traffic and long, straight sections, and the heat from June to September is extreme, often above fifty degrees. Spring and autumn are better, and winter days are mild and sometimes rainy.

Fuel is available on the main road, and in towns such as Nasiriyah and Al Fuhud, but in the marsh villages you rely on boats and local hospitality. If you are invited into a reed guesthouse, expect sweet tea, flatbread and perhaps fish from the water. Always check the latest official travel advice and local conditions before you plan to go.
t.historic sanctuary of machu picchu@-13.2:
Machu Picchu is the most famous place in the Andes, and it is also one of the hardest to reach for a rider, because no road goes there. The sanctuary is about thirty kilometres from Ollantaytambo, on a ridge nearly twenty-four hundred metres above the sea, above a loop of the Urubamba river, with cloud forest on every side. The citadel is reached only by train or by walking, and then by a bus up a zigzag road from the town of Aguas Calientes, at the foot of the mountain.

The Incas built it in the mid-fifteenth century, probably as a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti, with palaces, temples, terraces and fountains laid out around a central plaza, and the stonework fits so exactly that a knife blade will not slip between the blocks. It was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest and never found by the Spanish, which is why it survived. The American academic Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911, led by local farmers who already knew the place. UNESCO listed it in 1983, and today the site is limited by timed tickets, so book well ahead, and bring your passport.

Getting there by bike is part of the adventure. Many riders travel from Cusco through the Sacred Valley to Ollantaytambo, a good road with bends, villages and views of snowy peaks, then continue over the high pass of Abra Malaga, over four thousand metres, to the lowlands, and down a rough dirt road to the hydroelectric station. From there you walk the railway line for about ten kilometres, with trains passing, to Aguas Calientes. Surfaces are sometimes loose, landslides are common in the rainy season from December to March, and the altitude takes its toll, so give yourself a few days in Cusco to acclimatise.

Fuel and services are best bought in Urubamba or Cusco, and Ollantaytambo, a village of two thousand people, has cafes, hostels and a fine Inca fortress. Aguas Calientes has restaurants, hot springs and hotels, and prices are high. The dry season, from May to September, is the most popular, while April and October are quieter and still reasonably dry. Mornings bring mist that clears slowly, which is a wonderful time to be on the ruins.
t.hegmataneh@34.8,48.5:
Hamadan is one of the oldest cities in the world still lived in, and the hill at its heart is the site of Ecbatana, the capital of the Medes in the seventh century BC. The Greek historian Herodotus described the city as a series of seven concentric walls in different colours, with the royal treasure within the innermost, and later it became the summer capital of the Achaemenid kings, who came here to escape the heat of Persepolis and Susa. The mound, called Hegmataneh, is a low, wide hill within the modern city, and the excavations have revealed mud-brick walls and foundations, with a small museum on the site. It takes imagination to see the ancient city, but the place is a good introduction to the layers of Iranian history.

Hamadan stands at a height of about 1,800 metres, at the foot of Mount Alvand, a granite peak that rises above the city and holds snow into early summer. The air is cool, the summer is mild and winters are cold, which is why kings came here. Nearby, the Ganjnameh, a pair of inscriptions carved into the rock face by Darius and Xerxes, record in three languages their names and lineage. The tomb of Avicenna, the philosopher and physician, stands in the city centre, a modern monument that draws visitors from across the country.

Bisotun, the other half of this ride, lies on the road to the west, where a huge cliff carries the great relief and inscription of Darius I, the key to the decipherment of cuneiform. The landscape between them is a high plateau of wheat fields and walnut orchards.

Riding in Iran needs preparation, and the rules for foreign visitors, the paperwork for vehicles and the situation on the ground can change. Check current advice and permits before you plan a journey. In the city, traffic is dense and driving is assertive. Fuel stations are plentiful in Hamadan, Āzādshahr and the neighbouring towns, and the bazaar is a good place for a kebab and tea. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.segment choquecancha paucarpata@-13.0,-7:
Along the heights above the Sacred Valley of the Incas, a footpath of stone and earth winds across the mountains, and this is one tiny part of one of the greatest road systems ever built. The Qhapaq Ñan was the road network of the Inca empire, some thirty thousand kilometres of trail linking the coast, the Andes and the forests of what are now six countries. UNESCO listed it in 2014, and the Cusco region, the heart of the empire, has some of the best-preserved stretches, many of them with the original stone paving, steps cut into the rock and retaining walls that have survived five centuries of rain.

The road was a political tool as much as a trade route. Runners, the chasqui, carried messages in relay along it, and the army could march quickly from one end of the empire to the other. There were storehouses and rest stops along the way, and since the Incas had no wheeled vehicles, the paths are built for feet and llamas, with long flights of steps on steep sections.

None of this is a motorcycle road, of course; these segments are for walking. The bike gets you to the valley. Urubamba, at about 2,800 metres, is the natural base, with Calca, Pisac and Ollantaytambo along the same river. The highway through the valley is generally good tarmac, with long bends, mountain views and a lot of local traffic, including buses, trucks and mototaxis. Higher roads, including the climb over Abra Málaga, which reaches over four thousand metres, are far more demanding, with mist, hairpins and landslides in the rainy season, from November to March. The dry season from May to September is the best time, with brilliant mornings and very cold nights.

Fuel and supplies are easiest in Urubamba and Calca, towns of several thousand people. Choclo, the giant-kernel Andean corn, served with a slice of fresh cheese, is the classic roadside snack, and a pot of coca tea is a gentle help against altitude. Take your time, acclimatise for a couple of days before riding high, and respect the weather, which changes quickly in the mountains.
t.taj abad@34.9,48.2:
Western Iran's high plateau is a land of ancient roads, and the one that runs past Tāj Ābād is among the oldest. The village lies in Hamadan province, in the foothills below the Alvand massif, in a region the Medes once ruled from their capital Ecbatana, called Hegmataneh in Persian, now buried beneath the modern city of Hamadan, one of the oldest cities in Iran. Not far away, the cliff of Bisotun carries a huge inscription ordered by Darius I around 520 BC, telling in three languages how he took the throne, a text that helped scholars decode cuneiform in the nineteenth century. UNESCO listed it in 2006. I cannot tell you what stands at the exact point of the label, but I can describe the country around it.

The landscape is high and dry, a plateau at around two thousand metres, with fields of wheat and barley, orchards of walnut and apple, and bare ridges rising to snow-covered peaks. Alvand, east of Hamadan, rises to over three and a half thousand metres. Roads here are generally well surfaced and wide, with long climbs and curving descents through mountain passes. Winters are severe, with snow and ice, and summer days are hot and clear, while spring and autumn are the best seasons, with cool air and sharp light. Truck traffic is heavy on the main highways, so look well ahead on blind curves.

Asadābād, about fourteen kilometres away, is a town of nearly sixty thousand people, with fuel, bakeries and shops, and Bahār, with nearly thirty thousand, lies farther off. Fuel stations are common on the main roads, though queues and rationing rules can apply, so check locally. Travel conditions and entry rules for foreign visitors change, so look up current advice before you plan a route.

Hamadan has an old tradition of hospitality, and if you stop in a village you may well be offered tea and sweets. Try the local bread, the walnut sweets and the strong, sweet tea served in small glasses. Further on, the Ganjnameh inscriptions, carved by Darius and his son Xerxes in the rock above Hamadan, are another reminder that this land was a crossroads of empires long before the age of the motorcycle.
t.gar arjeneh rock shelter@33.4,48.3:
Khorramabad lies in a basin of the Zagros mountains, and the country around it is one of the oldest inhabited in Iran. The Gar Arjeneh rock shelter is only five kilometres from the city, in a land of limestone ridges, caves and oak forest that has attracted people for tens of thousands of years. The region of Lorestan is known for its caves, which have yielded evidence of early human occupation, including Neanderthal-era stone tools, and for the Luristan bronzes, a spectacular series of metalwork produced by local craftsmen in the first millennium BC.

The rock shelter is one of several prehistoric sites in the area, and the details of what was found there belong to archaeologists, so treat any visit with respect. Rock shelters are fragile places, and the rule everywhere is to look without disturbing. What you can say with confidence is that the Zagros foothills were a corridor for people and animals moving between the highlands and the plains of Mesopotamia, and that Lorestan's caves preserve a long record of that movement.

Khorramabad itself is a town of nearly three hundred and thirty thousand people, dominated by the Falak-ol-Aflak, a big castle on a rocky hill in the centre that dates from the Sasanian period and was rebuilt several times. It houses a museum of local archaeology and ethnography, and its walls look out over the town and the green valley. The Lur people, who live in the region, have a lively culture of music, nomadic traditions and cooking, and in spring you may see their herds moving to the high pastures.

The mountain roads around are scenic. They curve through oak woods, along river valleys and over high passes, with surfaces that vary from good to poor, and wide views of folded ridges. Spring is the best season, when the slopes are green and wildflowers are abundant. Winter brings snow and ice, and summer is hot in the valleys.

Fuel and food are plentiful in Khorramabad, and the city has a good bazaar. Check local conditions before heading into remote areas, and carry water.
t.the east hammar marshes@30.7,47.4:
The marshes of southern Iraq are one of the strangest places on earth to find in a desert. Where the Tigris and Euphrates come together in their last stretch before the Persian Gulf, the land is so flat that the water spreads out instead of flowing, forming a maze of reed beds, shallow lagoons and channels, some of them wide enough for a boat and others narrow enough to touch both banks. The East Hammar is one of the great blocks of marsh that survives here, a wide mosaic of reed and open water lying east of the Euphrates and close to the Iranian border. UNESCO inscribed the Ahwar of Southern Iraq in 2016, as both a natural wonder and the home of a unique culture.

That culture belongs to the Ma'dan, the Marsh Arabs, who for thousands of years have lived on floating islands of reed and in houses woven entirely from the same plant. Their great guest halls, the mudhif, are arched like cathedral naves in bundled reeds, and their water buffalo wade among the lilies. In the 1990s, the government of Saddam Hussein drained much of the marshes, to punish the people for the 1991 uprising and to remove a hiding place for rebels, and the area shrank to a fraction of its size. After 2003 the dikes were broken and the water came back, and many people returned, although reduced rainfall, upstream dams and salt are a continuing threat.

The birdlife is exceptional. The marshes are a wintering ground and a stopover on the route between Siberia and Africa, and they hold two species found almost nowhere else: the Basra reed warbler and the Iraq babbler. Pelicans, ibis and pygmy cormorants fill the sky in winter.

I cannot honestly describe a ride here in the usual way. Access to the marshes involves local guides, boats, permission and a realistic look at the security situation, and the summer heat, which can pass fifty degrees in July and August, is dangerous. The cooler months, from November to March, are the only sensible time.

The nearest town on the map is Al Hartha, north of Basra, a large place with fuel and markets, and Basra, a port city on the Shatt al-Arab, has everything. The ancient city of Ur, with its great ziggurat near Nasiriyah, is the other half of the ride list, and in a landscape this old it is natural that the two stand together.
t.queenstown@-45.0,168.7:
Queenstown has a reputation for adrenaline, but I think its best trick is the geography. The town sits on the shore of Lake Wakatipu, a long, dark, glacier-carved lake shaped like a lightning bolt, with the Remarkables mountain range rising straight from the far side in a wall of grey rock and snow. A Māori legend says the lake is the burnt outline of a giant, Matau, whose heart still beats under the water, and the lake level does rise and fall in a slow rhythm, a seiche caused by wind and pressure, which is the scientific explanation for the legend. The old coal-fired steamship TSS Earnslaw, launched in 1912, still crosses the lake to a high-country farm.

The gold rush brought the first crowds. In 1862 gold was found in the Arrow River, and the tiny town of Arrowtown boomed, with thousands of miners including a large group from China. The wooden cottages of the Chinese settlement have been restored, and the autumn colours of the poplars and birches along the river are famous in April and May. The modern age gave Queenstown its commercial bungy, which began at the Kawarau Bridge in 1988.

The Crown Range Road is why a rider is here. It climbs from the Wakatipu basin in a series of tight switchbacks with views down to Queenstown, then crosses a high saddle at 1,076 metres, the highest sealed main road in the country, before descending to the Cardrona valley and Wanaka. The surface is good, the corners are tight in the climb and open on top, and the views across the Pisa Range are huge. Ice and snow can close the road or require chains in winter, so check the conditions, and the temperature can drop ten degrees between town and summit. Take care on the descent, because oncoming vehicles and cyclists cut corners.

The best months are December to March for a dry road and long days, and April, when the leaves turn. Winter is for ski traffic and caution. The Cardrona Hotel, a gold rush-era pub on the other side of the pass, is a popular stop for a pie and a pint of local beer.

Queenstown has plenty of fuel stations and Arrowtown has a few too, so fill up in town before climbing, because the summit has no services.
t.segment abra choqetakarpu toroyoq@-13.7,:
Apurímac is a Quechua word that means the speaker of the gods, or the great speaker, and it is the name of the river whose canyon you cross, deep and loud, on any road between Cusco and Abancay. The region around Abancay is one of the least visited in the southern Andes, and I find that its character is mostly vertical: valleys at 2,000 metres with sugar cane and avocados, then switchbacks climbing into puna grassland above 4,000 metres where the wind is cold and the llamas look at you without interest. The abra in the title, Spanish for a mountain pass, is one of those high crossings, and the Inca road, the Qhapaq Ñan, runs over or near it.

The Qhapaq Ñan was the road system of the Inca empire, some 30,000 kilometres of paved and stepped paths linking Colombia to Chile and Argentina, with relay stations, storehouses and bridges. Runners called chasquis carried messages along it at astonishing speed, handing knotted cords from one post to the next. A large part of the network was listed by UNESCO in 2014, across six countries, and this stretch in Apurímac is among the sections where the original stone paving and stairs survive. I cannot point you to a precise spot from the labels alone, so treat the segment as a walking route through high country, best explored on foot from a village with a local guide.

For a rider, the roads of Apurímac are among the more demanding in Peru. The highway from Cusco to Abancay is paved but twisting, with hairpins, landslide patches, trucks and the occasional herd of sheep, and the side roads leading to high passes are often gravel, rutted and steep. Altitude is the first thing to respect: at over 4,000 metres, engines lose power and riders get headaches, so acclimatise in Cusco for a couple of days and carry coca tea or ibuprofen as the locals do. The dry season, from May to September, is the time to go, with clear, cold mornings and frosts at night. From December to March, rain turns tracks to mud and the mist can come down without warning.

Fuel is the practical issue. Abancay, a city of over fifty thousand, has stations, and so do the larger towns on the main road, but villages in the high country may have none. Fill up in Abancay and carry extra if you head onto the side roads.

Take warm layers, even in daytime, and plenty of water. The silence at the top of a pass is almost physical.
t.manu national park@-12.2,-71.7:
Manú is arguably the richest place on the planet for living things, and it earns that status through a single, dizzying slope. The national park runs from the high grasslands of the Andes at over 4,000 metres down through cloud forest and into the lowland Amazon rainforest, at about 300 metres, in a few dozen kilometres, and each step of the way holds different life. More than a thousand species of birds have been recorded, along with jaguars, giant otters, tapirs, spider monkeys and uncounted insects. UNESCO listed it in 1987 and the core zone is closed to visitors, with a few Indigenous groups living in voluntary isolation.

The Cock-of-the-rock is the park's celebrity. Males of this bird, bright orange with a crest like a helmet, gather in the cloud forest at dawn to display, calling and bobbing in a loud, croaking chorus, and watching them from a hide on the Kosñipata road is a highlight for birders.

The road is the reason a rider might be here. From Cusco, the route heads over the high pass of Acjanaco, at well over 3,500 metres, then falls in a long series of bends through cloud forest to Pilcopata and Atalaya, where the road ends and the river takes over. It is a famously dramatic descent. The road is mostly unpaved, narrow, and clings to cliffs with huge drops, and landslides are common in the rainy season from November to March. Fog and rain are frequent, the surface is slick, and trucks and buses take the corners wide. It is not a road for beginners, and some stretches are closed or one-way at certain hours. Check conditions before setting out.

The dry months from May to September are the only sensible time, and even then, a downpour can come out of nowhere. The temperature goes from near freezing at the pass to steamy at the bottom, so layers are essential.

For fuel, fill up in Cusco and carry a spare can, because supplies in the lowland villages are uncertain. Entry to the park proper requires a licensed operator and a permit, and travellers go by boat from Atalaya, but the road itself is open to riders. Birdsong at dawn, a mist that lifts off the canopy, and the rumble of a river below: it is a place that makes you whisper.
t.prehistoric sites of the khorramabad val:
Khorramabad sits in a valley of the Zagros mountains in western Iran, in the province of Lorestan, and it is older than most people realise. The Kaldar Cave and several neighbouring sites in the valley hold evidence of human presence stretching back tens of thousands of years, to the Middle Palaeolithic, when Neanderthal people hunted wild goat and gazelle in these hills and sheltered in the limestone caves. The valley is a rare window into the deep past of the Iranian plateau, and UNESCO has recognised its significance.

The city itself is a lively place of over three hundred thousand people, with fuel, markets, restaurants and hotels, so practical needs are easy. Its most striking building is Falak-ol-Aflak, an old fortress on a rocky hill that rises above the town, now used as a museum, with displays of the bronzes that made Lorestan famous. The Lorestan bronzes, small, elaborate objects of animals and horse gear from the early first millennium BC, are some of the most beautiful metal craft from the ancient Near East. Nearby, the Shapuri Bridge, a Sasanian structure across the Khorramabad river, still holds some of its old arches.

The riding in Lorestan is among the best in the country. The roads lead through steep wooded valleys and over mountain passes, with long bends and views across oak-covered slopes, and in spring the hills are covered in flowers, with nomads moving their flocks to the high pastures. The tarmac is mostly good on the main routes, narrower and rougher on the side roads, and snow can close high passes from late autumn until spring. Keep an eye out for livestock, rockfalls after rain, and trucks on the main road from Arak and Dorud.

Lorestan is home to the Lurs, a people with their own language, music and traditions, and the hospitality here is warm and unforced. Tea is offered everywhere, and a polite refusal is sometimes less successful than accepting graciously.

The best time to come is April to June, when the hills are green and the temperature is pleasant, or September and October, when the light turns golden. Summers are hot in the valley bottom but cooler in the mountains, and winters are cold and snowy. If you are interested in the caves, ask at the museum about access, as some sites require permission or a local guide, and the paths can be rough.
t.el calafate@-50.3,-72.3:
El Calafate is a small town on the southern shore of Lago Argentino, and it is almost entirely about one thing: the ice. Eighty kilometres west, in Los Glaciares National Park, the Perito Moreno Glacier pushes out of the Andes into the lake in a wall of blue ice about five kilometres wide, rising to some seventy metres above the water. Unlike most glaciers it is relatively stable, and every few years it advances far enough to dam an arm of the lake, until the pressure of water breaks through in a roaring collapse. Watching blocks of ice calve from the face and crash into the lake, with a sound like thunder delayed by a second, is one of the great sights of Patagonia.

The town itself is a pleasant base, with wooden buildings, restaurants serving lamb roasted over open fires and shops selling chocolate and woollens. It takes its name from the calafate bush, whose dark berries are made into jam and ice cream, and local legend says that anyone who eats them will return to Patagonia. Nearby, the Laguna Nimez nature reserve shelters flamingos, geese and other birds on the lake shore.

The ride here, on the Ruta 40 through Patagonia, is a test of endurance more than technique. The wind is relentless, often blowing at gale strength across the open steppe, and it is the main challenge for riders, pushing bikes sideways and making long straights exhausting. Distances between towns are large, and fuel is spread thin, so fill the tank at every opportunity. Parts of the route are gravel, though much has been paved in recent years, and sudden weather changes can bring rain, sleet or even snow in summer.

Calafate itself has everything a traveller needs, including several stations, supermarkets, banks and workshops, and an airport that brings in visitors from around the world. The best time is from November to March, with long daylight hours and warmer temperatures. Even then, bring warm gear and a windproof layer.
t.lindis pass and tekapo photo pull off@-4:
Not a single road reaches this pin. The coordinates lie deep in Fiordland, on the wild coast north of Milford Sound, in country of rainforest, rivers and mountains that has hardly changed since before people arrived. The nearest way in is a walking track, the Hollyford, which runs for days through the valley to the sea at Martins Bay, and the nearest roads stop well short of it. The ride is named for the Lindis Pass and Tekapo, which lie a long way east, so take this stop as a nod to the wilderness behind the road.

Fiordland is one of the wettest places on Earth, with rainfall of several metres a year, and the forests are thick with ferns, moss and beech. Waterfalls pour from the cliffs after rain, and the fjords are among the deepest in the world. The area is protected as a national park and part of the Te Wāhipounamu World Heritage Area, and the dense bush shelters rare birds such as the kākā and, in remote valleys, the takahē. For the riders who pass on the Milford Road, the nearby Homer Tunnel, a rough-hewn passage through the rock, is the gateway.

The riding that this ride actually offers is the Lindis Pass, on State Highway 8 between Omarama and Tarras, a crossing of about nine hundred and seventy metres through golden tussock hills. The road climbs in long, easy curves and falls away to the Mackenzie Basin, with its wide plains, turquoise lakes and the white peaks of the Southern Alps. At Lake Tekapo, the little stone Church of the Good Shepherd, built in 1935, stands on the shore, and the sky above is among the darkest in the world, part of an international dark sky reserve.

Fuel is the thing to plan for. Omarama, Tarras and Tekapo all have stations, but they are far apart, so fill the tank at each opportunity. In winter, snow and ice can close the Lindis Pass, and chains may be needed. Summer is warm and dry, with the Mackenzie blue with lupins in November and December. If you can, stay for the stars at Tekapo, which are astonishing.
t.queenstown south island@-44.4,169.5:
Lake Hawea lies in a long trough between the mountains, and this pin sits in the high country behind it, in the wild country of the Hunter valley. The lake itself is a deep blue, ringed with brown hills in summer and white peaks in winter, and it is smaller and quieter than its neighbour, Lake Wānaka, which lies just across a low neck of land. The lake level was raised in the 1950s by a dam at its outlet, drowning old shorelines and giving the water its present form.

The Haast Pass Highway, State Highway 6, runs along the lake's edge before climbing into the mountains, and it is one of the great rides of the South Island. From Hawea, the road follows the lake's shore with moderate bends and views across the water, then passes through the settlement of Makarora and climbs over the Haast Pass, at five hundred and sixty-three metres, one of the lowest crossings of the Southern Alps. On the western side, the road drops through rainforest to the coast, with waterfalls and gorges on the way.

The mountains here are the heart of the Southern Alps, with snow on the peaks for much of the year and glaciers in the highest basins. The Hunter valley, behind the lake, is a remote area of tussock, beech forest and braided rivers, with a few huts for hikers and anglers. The air is clear and cold, and the water in the lake is glacial, so swimming is brisk, even in the middle of summer. A dip in the shallows on a hot day is a good way to wake up.

For fuel, fill in Wānaka or Hawea before heading toward the pass, as supplies on the road are limited. Makarora has a small shop and cafe, and the next stations are on the west coast, a long way off. In winter, ice and snow can affect the road, and sandflies on the west side can be fierce in summer, so carry repellent. Spring and autumn offer the best light, and the colours of the larches in May are striking.
t.queenstown south island@-44.3,169.0:
Lake Wānaka narrows toward its head into a landscape that mountaineers call the gateway to Mount Aspiring, and the pin sits somewhere in the folded country at the top of it, in the wild lands of the national park. The lake is long, deep and glacial, a cold turquoise in summer, with steep brown hills falling to its shores and snow-capped peaks beyond. The air here is clear, the silence is deep, and the only sounds are wind, water and birdsong.

The Makarora valley, which runs north from the head of the lake, is the first stage of the Haast Pass route, and beech forest, braided rivers and open flats line the road. The Māori used the pass as a route to the west coast for pounamu, and early explorers followed in the 1860s. The mountains of the Southern Alps are formed by the collision of two tectonic plates and are still rising, at several millimetres a year, while erosion wears them down.

The ride on the road to the pass is magnificent, and a swim in the lake is a bracing way to break it. The water is glacial and cold, rarely above fifteen degrees even in summer, but on a warm afternoon it is wonderfully refreshing. Look for shingle beaches with easy access, and stay close to the shore. Trout fishing is also popular, and the rivers are clear, with fish visible in the pools.

For fuel, fill in Wānaka before heading north, since there are no stations on the road until the west coast. Makarora has a small shop and cafe. Sandflies are fierce near water, so carry repellent. Winter can bring snow and ice, and the road may require chains, so check conditions before you go. In summer, the long evenings are warm, and the light on the mountains lasts well into the night.
t.crown range road@-45.0,168.9:
The Crown Range Road is the highest sealed public road in New Zealand, topping out at about a thousand and seventy-six metres, and it connects Queenstown with Wānaka by a route that is as beautiful as it is steep. The pin lies near the top, between Arrowtown and the Cardrona valley, where the road crosses a high saddle of tussock and bare rock. On one side, the land falls away toward the Wakatipu basin, with the jagged line of the Remarkables across the valley. On the other, the Cardrona valley opens, golden and broad, leading toward Wānaka.

The Cardrona Hotel, built in 1863 during the gold rush, still stands at the foot of the descent, with a long veranda, a garden and a reputation for good food, and it is a favourite stop for riders and skiers. The valley once held a town of thousands, and the remains of the gold workings can be seen along the roadside. In winter, the ski fields of Cardrona and Treble Cone draw crowds, and the road carries a stream of cars with skis on the roof.

The ride is excellent. From Arrowtown, the road climbs in a series of tight zigzags known as the Zig Zag, with views over the town and the valley, and then crosses the high plateau before descending to Cardrona. The surface is good, but the road is narrow, with steep drop-offs and few barriers, and snow and ice make it dangerous in winter, when chains are required. In summer, the days are warm and clear, and the air is dry. Take care on the hairpins, where the road may be shaded and damp.

Fuel is available at Arrowtown, Queenstown and Wānaka, but not on the road, so fill up before you go. The hotel at Cardrona offers food and drink, and a stop there is part of the experience. Check weather and road conditions before setting out, since the pass can close in snow. Carry warm clothing, even in summer, and watch for cyclists on the climb.
t.queenstown south island@-44.4,168.6:
Mount Aspiring, called Tititea by Māori, is the pyramid of ice and rock that dominates the western Otago ranges, and the pin lies in the wilderness just to its west. At just over three thousand metres, it is the highest peak in New Zealand outside the Aoraki Mount Cook region, and its steep faces and hanging glaciers attract mountaineers from around the world. No road comes near the pin. It sits in the national park, among beech forest, river flats and high basins, a landscape that few people ever see.

The part of the country that a rider can reach lies to the south, at the head of Lake Wakatipu, near Glenorchy. From there, the road runs north through the Rees valley toward Paradise, a stretch of about twenty kilometres of gravel through farmland and beech forest, with the mountains standing around like a wall. The area was used as a film location for The Lord of the Rings, and the landscape does look like Middle-earth. The gravel is generally good, though loose in places, and the fords can be deep after rain.

The lake is the other theme. Lake Wakatipu is shaped like a lightning bolt, and its water level rises and falls by a few centimetres every half hour, a phenomenon that locals explain with a legend about a giant whose heart beats beneath the water. Scientists have a less romantic answer, but the legend is more fun. The water is cold, around ten degrees even in summer, and a swim is for the brave, but the stony beaches at the head of the lake are beautiful.

Fuel is not available at the head of the lake, so fill the tank in Queenstown before the run to Glenorchy, which is about forty-five kilometres. A cafe in Glenorchy serves coffee and pies, and the village has a small general store. Be careful on the gravel, and check river levels before crossing fords. Autumn brings golden poplars and clear light, and winter brings snow on the peaks.
t.glenorchy lake road@-44.6,168.1:
The Routeburn Track, one of New Zealand's Great Walks, climbs from the Routeburn valley near Glenorchy, over a high saddle and down to the Divide on the Milford Road, and this pin lies in the mountains close to its line. No road reaches it. The country here is high, wet and wild, with beech forest, alpine lakes and jagged peaks, and the Humboldt mountains stand over it like a wall. A rider arrives on the lake road and looks up at it from below.

Glenorchy is the end of the road, a village of a few hundred people at the head of Lake Wakatipu, named by Scottish settlers in the 1860s after a glen in Scotland. The village has a cafe, a pub, a small shop and a lagoon with boardwalks and birdlife, and it is the gateway to some of the finest walking in the country. A handful of tour operators run jet boats and horse treks, and in autumn the poplars along the road turn gold, making the place glow.

The lake road itself is one of the great rides of the South Island. It runs for forty-odd kilometres from Queenstown, hugging the shore in a series of bends, with the water on one side and steep hills on the other, and the views of the lake and the peaks beyond are superb. The surface is good, but the road is narrow and winding, with sheer drops in places, and it can be busy with tour buses in summer. In the morning, mist lies over the lake, and the light is soft.

For food, Glenorchy has a few simple places to eat, so a stop for lunch is easy, though there may be a wait in the busy season. Fill up in Queenstown, since fuel at the head of the lake is limited, and carry layers, as the weather changes quickly. Sandflies are common near the water, so bring repellent. The light in the evening, with the mountains turning pink and the lake still, is a fine reward.
t.milford road expedition@-44.9,168.9:
Start with the number everyone asks about: the Crown Range road, which climbs out of the Cardrona valley, tops out at 1,076 metres and is usually described as the highest sealed main road in New Zealand. These coordinates sit in the Cardrona valley itself, just short of that climb, with Arrowtown about ten kilometres off and Queenstown a little over twenty-five. It is wide, open farmland in a bowl of brown hills, and in winter the ski fields above turn the whole valley white.

Milford Road is the destination the ride is named after, and a rider should understand what that means before leaving. Queenstown and Wanaka are the proper places to fill up before a long day on this side of the island, and this valley is a fine place to check the gauge and tyre pressures rather than a place to buy anything. The Homer Tunnel at the end is a one-way, unlit bore blasted through granite, and in snow season the road can close for avalanche control.

The Cardrona itself has a past worth knowing. Gold was found in the river in the 1860s, and the valley filled with miners, shopkeepers and the pubs that serve them. A hotel from that era still stands by the road and is a favourite with photographers, with a veranda to match and an open fire in cold weather. Bikers have been stopping there for coffee for longer than most of us have been riding.

The road south over the Crown Range is the highlight of the day: a series of tight hairpins climbing out of the valley, a short, fast ridge at the top with views across to the Remarkables, and then a long descent in switchbacks toward Arrowtown. It is twisty, narrow in places, and very popular with campervans in summer, so patience pays. Early morning is the quiet hour, before the sun hits the frost on the shaded bends, and the light on the schist hills is sublime. Gusts on the summit can be fierce, and there is no barrier on some drops. Respect the signs and the weather forecast.
t.queenstown south island@-44.6,168.3:
Look at a map and this point sits in the middle of nowhere: high above the head waters of the Dart and Rees valleys, in the wild mountain country between Lake Wakatipu and Mount Aspiring. There is no road here, not even a good track for a bike, only ice, rock and bush on the slopes of peaks like Earnslaw, whose snow-capped summit dominates the horizon from Glenorchy. The label calls it a return to Queenstown, which tells you what the route does: it brings you home, and the actual road runs far to the east.

What exists here is landscape on a vast scale. The Southern Alps forced upward by the grinding of the Pacific and Australian plates, and the glaciers that carved the lakes are still cutting valleys in the high basins. Beech forest covers the lower slopes, and keas, the alpine parrots with a taste for rubber and a character to match, patrol the ridges. Tramping tracks like the Rees-Dart loop pass nearby on foot, taking several days, and a hiker who left the roadhead at Glenorchy sees none of what the motorcyclist sees from the road.

The riding that does lead you toward this region is the run around Lake Wakatipu, one of the best short rides in the country. Between Queenstown and Glenorchy the road is narrow, curving, and full of lake views, and the mountains close in with every kilometre. From Glenorchy it carries on to the gravel, so unless you are riding something built for dirt, the tarmac ends and the turn-around begins. Rental riders in particular should check the conditions of their contract before heading up any unsealed road.

For fuel and food you will want Queenstown, a lively resort town with plenty of everything and a petrol station on most main roads. Glenorchy has a small store and a cafe or two but is not the place to assume anything about fuel, so fill the tank before leaving town. Evenings in the high country cool off quickly, even in mid-summer, and rain can arrive from the west with hardly any notice.

If you end up at this spot in the sense of looking at it from the road, you are most likely seeing it as a distant white wall. Treat it that way: a backdrop, and a very good one.
t.mount cook high country photo pull off@-:
Mount Cook is a long way off from here, more than a hundred kilometres to the north-east, and the ride's name only promises a view of the range. What these coordinates actually give you is the Matukituki side of Lake Wanaka: sheep paddocks, braided glacial river, and a wall of the Southern Alps closing the valley at its head. Wanaka lies about thirty kilometres to the east and Arrowtown a bit further, so the pull-off sits in empty country between the two.

The road up the Matukituki valley starts as good tarmac from Wanaka, runs along the lake past Glendhu Bay, and then turns to gravel for the final stretch, with a couple of creek fords that rise after rain. It ends at a car park beneath the Mount Aspiring massif, a pyramid of rock and ice that locals call the Matterhorn of the South, for obvious reasons. Riders on heavy touring bikes may well stop at the gravel and be content with the views; adventure bikes can go on, with a look at the fords first.

Geology is the story of this valley. A glacier carved a deep trough in the schist during the ice ages, and the Matukituki River now wanders over a wide gravel bed it cannot fill, changing channel after every flood. The lake itself, Wanaka, is the fourth largest in the country and is fed by that same river. In late afternoon the light turns the schist slopes copper, and the tussock glows. Kea sometimes visit car parks looking for loose rubber, so keep an eye on your panniers.

Wanaka has fuel, food and a good lakeside walk, and is where to stock up, since the valley itself has none. In summer the town is busy with holidaymakers and the traffic out to Glendhu Bay can be slow, so go early. Winter brings ice to the shaded corners, and snow can close the higher roads for a day or two.

The farm stations here date back to the first runholders of the 1860s, who drove merino sheep into the high country and later suffered brutal winters and rabbit plagues. Their woolsheds still dot the valleys. A road like this one is as much about that long human history as the mountains, and a rider with an eye for old stone chimneys will spot a few.
t.haast pass west coast photo pull off@-44:
Look at the map and this point lands deep in Fiordland, on the wet western side of the Southern Alps, nowhere near the Haast Pass road the ride is named for. No road reaches it. It sits in the rainforest and rock between the Hollyford and the Darran Mountains, in some of the wettest country on earth, where Milford Sound collects around six metres of rain in a typical year. Waterfalls appear on every cliff after a downpour and vanish the day after.

The genuine Haast Pass is a different thing, and a lovely one. At 563 metres it is one of the lowest crossings of the Southern Alps, linking Wanaka and the Otago lakes to the West Coast through beech forest and past a succession of waterfalls, the Fantail and the Thunder Creek falls being the best known. The road follows the Makarora and then the Haast rivers down to the coast, passing blue pools and river flats where the water runs the colour of milk and pale jade. The highway was only completed in the 1960s, so for generations the West Coast had to be reached by sea or mountain track.

For the rider, Haast is wonderfully easy by alpine standards: wide, smooth, with long relaxed bends and little traffic. What bites is the weather. West of the main divide it can rain for days, the sandflies are fierce at every stop, and low cloud will hide the peaks you came for. Ride it on a settled forecast and keep the rain gear on top of the pannier. Towns are far apart. There is fuel at Wanaka, and at Haast on the coast, but the long stretch between is empty, so fill up before you leave and treat any pump on the way as a bonus rather than a plan.

The old Maori route over the pass was a greenstone trail, for pounamu is found on the West Coast and was carried east in small, treasured pieces. Early European explorers like Julius von Haast, after whom the pass is named, spent a good deal of effort finding what the Maori already knew.

As for this particular spot, treat it as a reminder of the scale of the country. The Fiordland ranges stand to the south-west, impenetrable and unlogged, and a rider looking at them from the road is looking at one of the great wildernesses of the Southern Hemisphere.
t.nazca@-14.8,-74.9:
Nazca sits in the middle of one of the driest places on earth, a small desert town of about twenty-four thousand people on the Pan-American Highway, famous for lines drawn in the ground that nobody quite agrees on. The Nazca Lines, a collection of enormous figures and straight lines scratched into the stony plain, were made between about two thousand and fifteen hundred years ago by removing dark surface pebbles to expose the pale ground beneath. Birds, a monkey, a spider, a hummingbird: they were drawn on a scale that can only be appreciated from the air, and in 1994 they were listed as a World Heritage site.

The explanations are many. Some say astronomical calendars, others say ritual paths, others say water, and one German mathematician, Maria Reiche, spent most of her life here measuring and sweeping the lines clean. Her house is a museum, and she is remembered with real affection in town. The desert's dry, windless climate is what has preserved the markings, though a rare rainstorm is a worry to the guardians.

For riders the best free look is the viewing tower beside the highway north of town, a rickety metal lookout that gives a glimpse of a couple of the figures. Proper sightseeing means a small plane from the airfield, which is a bumpy, nauseating and thrilling half hour. If you plan it, go early in the morning before the thermals build up. The region has other treasures too: ancient aqueducts, spiralling underground channels that still feed the farms, and the desert cemeteries where mummies lie in the dry sand.

The riding here is long and straight, with enormous distances between towns, brown mountains and no shade. The road from Ica comes across dry plateaus and the wind is variable, often strong in the afternoon. The temperature climbs hard through the day, so drink more water than seems sensible, and start early. Fuel is easy to find in Nazca itself, a proper town with garages on the main road, restaurants serving grilled chicken and ceviche, and plenty of hostels, though it is wise to top up before heading south on the next stage towards Camana, where distances between pumps grow again.

When the sun goes down the desert cools fast, and the stars here are thick and brilliant. A rider with a camera should save a little energy for that.
t.cerro castillo chile@-51.3,-72.3:
Cerro Castillo is a tiny settlement on the Patagonian steppe in the Magallanes region of southern Chile, close to the Argentine border, and it is the last place of any size on the road from Puerto Natales to the Torres del Paine national park. Around it the land is a vast sweep of tawny grass, scrub and low hills, broken by lakes and rivers and a long horizon with snowy peaks far off to the west. It looks empty, and it is not: guanacos graze in small herds beside the road, rheas dash through the grass, and condors circle on the thermals.

The wind is the character of Patagonia. It blows steadily from the west and gusts hard across the open plain, and on a motorbike it demands constant attention, leaning the bike into each gust and bracing for the moments when the wind drops or changes direction. A bike with a full-face helmet and good luggage security is worth the effort, and the days are long in summer, with light until late in the evening. The sheep estancias that dot the landscape are the economic backbone of the region, and the road passes the long fences and old wool sheds that tell of the nineteenth-century boom.

The road from Puerto Natales runs north on Route 9 and then turns toward the park on a good paved road, although some sections beyond may be gravel, and conditions change with the season. Fuel is the key practical point: fill the tank in Puerto Natales, which is the nearest town of size and about an hour from here, because services in this area are scarce and the distances are long. A small roadside stop may offer a coffee or a sandwich.

Weather in Patagonia can change in minutes. Sun, rain, hail and wind can appear in a single hour, so waterproofs and layers are essential. The best season is from November to March, when roads are open and the days are long.
