As you approach the park, the first sight of the jagged Paine peaks over the plain is a moment worth stopping for.
t.laguna amarga@-51.0,-72.7:
Laguna Amarga is the entrance to Torres del Paine, and the first view of the park's famous towers makes the whole long journey seem worth it. The lagoon itself is a shallow, brackish lake of milky green water on the open steppe, ringed by low hills, and behind it rise the granite spires of the Paine massif, three vertical towers of rock that seem to belong in another country. The name means bitter lake, from the salty water.

The park is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and in this corner of it the wildlife is easy to spot. Guanacos, the wild relatives of the llama, graze beside the road with a calm indifference to vehicles, and rheas and foxes appear in the grass. Condors are frequent visitors, circling the cliffs at midday. The Paine river runs through a lovely valley beside the entrance, and the wind sweeps across it constantly.

There is a ranger station at the entrance where visitors register and pay the park fee, and this is where the day's ride ends. From here, trails lead into the mountains toward the base of the towers, and a road continues on to Lake Pehoé and the Grey glacier area. The track beyond the entrance is mostly gravel, and the surface can be rough with washboard and loose stones, so ride carefully and give yourself plenty of time.

Fuel is one thing you should plan for in advance. There is no station at the entrance, and the nearest reliable place to fill the tank is Puerto Natales, around two hours' ride to the south. Carrying a little extra in a safe container is common practice, and it pays to start any day in the park with a full tank. A small shop and a lodge near the entrance may offer food and drink, but supplies are limited.

The best time to visit is from November to March, in the long southern summer, but the weather is always unpredictable. Cold wind, sudden rain and bright sun can all arrive within an hour, so dress in layers and bring good waterproofs. Early in the morning, with the light low and the wind often at its calmest, the towers glow orange, and it is easily one of the most memorable sights in South America.
t.chicamocha canyon@6.8,-73.0:
The Chicamocha is one of the great canyons of South America, and the road along its edge has a scale that surprises people who think of Colombia as green and gentle. The river has cut a gorge in the Santander mountains that is more than a kilometre deep in places and stretches for over two hundred kilometres, a dry, rugged landscape of cactus, scrub and layers of rock in shades of ochre, red and grey. Locals will tell you it is among the biggest canyons in the world, and the view from the rim makes you believe it.

The highway between Bucaramanga and San Gil descends into the canyon in a long series of bends, crosses the river on a bridge, and climbs out the other side. The surface is generally paved and in reasonable condition, but trucks are frequent, and the heat in the canyon bottom can be fierce. The upper rim is cool and windy, with a very different climate, and the temperature drop between the two is dramatic. The sun is strong and the air dry, so carry water.

At the viewpoints along the rim there are cafes and a national park with a cable car, a gondola that carries visitors across the canyon from one rim to the other, with the river a thin glittering thread far below. It is a thrilling ride for those who like heights, and the views are enormous. The area has a food tradition of its own, notably roast goat, which is eaten in the cafes along the road, and the local sweets made with fruit and sugar.

The hamlets nearby, such as Cepitá and Aratoca, are tiny, and fuel is not something to count on in them. The sensible places to fill the tank are Piedecuesta, a big town on the Bucaramanga side with some eighty thousand people, and San Gil on the other. Check the tank before you start the descent, because distances are long and the road is demanding.

The indigenous Guane people once lived in this region, and their stonework and rock paintings survive in places. The best light is in the morning and late afternoon, when the canyon walls turn gold, and the middle of the day is hot and hazy. Take care on the bends, where trucks can drift wide, and enjoy one of the great rides of the Andes.
t.san gil@6.6,-73.1:
San Gil calls itself the adventure capital of Colombia, and it earns the title with rivers, caves and cliffs in every direction. The town sits in the Santander hills above the Fonce river, near its meeting with the Suárez, and the rapids on both are among the best in the country for rafting. Paragliders launch from the ridges above the canyon, and cavers explore the limestone passages nearby. After a morning on the road, the shops offering tours look more tempting than the usual souvenir stalls.

The town itself is easy and pleasant, with a leafy central plaza, a handsome stone cathedral, and a park called El Gallineral on an island in the Fonce, where the trees are draped in long, silvery strands of a plant locally called barba de viejo, old man's beard, which gives the garden a ghostly beauty. Walking beneath them with the river sliding past is one of the town's pleasures, and a small entrance fee keeps the park well tended.

Nearby is the village of Barichara, about twenty kilometres away, which many consider the prettiest in Colombia, with white-washed houses, stone-paved streets and a calm that has scarcely changed in a century. It is easily reached on a short, well-paved road, and the route that connects the two is a lovely half-hour ride through dry hills and rock outcrops, with views over the canyon. A stone path, the Camino Real, leads on to the village of Guane, an old walk used by traders.

With more than thirty thousand people San Gil is the major service town of the region, and there is fuel, food and every kind of shop. The food is hearty, with the local speciality being roast goat, arepas and fried ants, a Santander curiosity, though it is hardly obligatory. The climate is warm, around twenty-five degrees in the day, and showers are frequent in the rainy seasons, so keep a jacket handy.

As a rest stop on the Chicamocha route, the town is a convenient and cheerful place. Traffic in the centre can be busy, especially on weekends, but the pace is easy, and a few quiet hours by the river make a fine pause.
t.embalse el yeso@-33.7,-70.1:
Embalse El Yeso is a reservoir in the high Andes, an hour or two above the last village of the Cajón del Maipo, and its colour alone is enough to make riders brake. The water is a shade of turquoise that seems artificial, held in a bowl of bare brown mountains with snow patches on the heights and the cone of Volcán San José standing guard at nearly six thousand metres. The dam was built in the 1960s to supply drinking water to Santiago, and the lake is still a vital source for the capital, which is why access is controlled and swimming is not allowed.

The approach is half the pleasure. From San José de Maipo, the road follows the river upstream through a narrowing canyon, past little settlements, orchards and hot-spring resorts, with steep walls of red and ochre rock rising on both sides. After the paved section ends, the last stretch to the reservoir is a gravel track that climbs through switchbacks to around 2,500 metres. Expect washboard, loose stones and dust, and be careful when passing vehicles. It is a route better suited to an adventure bike than a road racer.

The air at this height is thin, dry and cold, and the sun is fierce. Condors are sometimes seen riding the thermals above the ridges, and guanacos and foxes live among the scree. In summer, wildflowers colour the slopes, and the light is very clear. In winter the road closes under snow, and the whole valley is often closed to vehicles from late autumn into spring, so check conditions before you go. Entry to the reservoir area may require a permit or a guided tour, so confirm before planning a visit.

Simple cafés in the lower valley serve empanadas and grilled meat, and weekends bring crowds from the city. Go on a weekday if you can, and aim to be back below the high ground before dark.
t.villa de leyva@5.6,-73.5:
Villa de Leyva was founded in 1572 and has barely changed since. At 2,140 metres, on a dry plateau in the Boyacá highlands, the town is a grid of whitewashed houses with red roofs, set around one of the largest cobbled plazas in the Americas, a great open square of rounded stones with a simple stone fountain in the middle and a church at one end. On a clear day, with the sun on the white walls and the mountains behind, the effect is almost theatrical.

The town was named for Andrés Díaz Venero de Leyva, the first president of the Royal Audience of New Granada, and it served as a retreat for colonial officials and later for independence-era families. Colombia has protected it as a national monument since the 1950s, which is why the streets are cobbled, wires are discreet and new building is strictly controlled. Nearby, the landscape tells older stories. The dry hills were once seabed, and fossils of marine reptiles, including a huge Kronosaurus, have been found in the area, while El Infiernito, a site of standing stones, was used by the Muisca people to observe the sun.

For riders, the road to Villa de Leyva climbs from the main highway through dry, scrubby hills with views over green valleys, a fun and flowing route with gentle curves and mixed surface quality. The cobbles in town are rough and slippery after rain, and the old streets are narrow, so go slowly, park and walk. The climate is mild and dry compared with much of the Colombian Andes, with sunny days and cool nights, and the best time to visit is between December and March or July and August.

Fuel is available in town, and larger towns like Tunja, about an hour away, have more services. The streets around the plaza are lined with cafés, bakeries and restaurants offering local dishes, from stews to arepas and fresh juices. Weekends bring crowds of visitors from Bogotá, so a weekday is calmer. Take time to walk the lanes at dusk, when the light turns gold and the town looks as though it were painted.
t.cristo redentor pass@-32.8,-70.1:
At 3,832 metres, the old pass between Argentina and Chile is one of the high points of South American riding, in more than one sense. It is a bare saddle of rock and scree on the border, with thin air, a hard wind and a statue of Christ the Redeemer standing on a plinth, arm raised, facing both countries. The monument was erected in 1904 to celebrate a peace agreement between the two nations after a long dispute over their frontier, and the bronze figure has been a symbol of friendship ever since.

Most traffic now goes through the long tunnel beneath the mountain, which opened in the 1980s and is a fixed link on the Mendoza to Santiago route. The old road over the top is a far smaller affair, rough and steep, and it is usually open only in the warm months and when conditions allow. It climbs from the Argentine side in a series of tight turns on gravel and broken tarmac, with steep drops and little protection. Check the status before you try it, and expect to turn back if snow or wind makes it unsafe. The Chilean side drops through a famous sequence of switchbacks, known as Los Caracoles, on a better road that connects to the Aconcagua valley.

The history is as high as the pass. In 1817, General José de San Martín led his Army of the Andes through passes near here to attack the Spanish in Chile, an extraordinary feat of logistics through snow and cold, with thousands of men, mules and cannon. The route was part of the campaign that led to Chilean independence, and the memory of it runs through both countries.

Uspallata on the Argentine side and Los Andes on the Chilean side are the places to fill the tank. Border formalities can take hours at the tunnel, particularly in summer and at weekends, so bring documents for you and the bike, patience and some food and water.

The cold is brutal even in summer, and the wind can knock a bike sideways. The best conditions are a still, clear morning, when the peaks around you stand out with total clarity.
t.pudeto@-51.1,-73.0:
Pudeto is a jetty, a car park and a thunderous little waterfall, and it earns its place in Torres del Paine for one reason: the view. The lake beside it is Pehoé, a startling milky turquoise made by glacial flour, and across the water the Cuernos del Paine, the Horns, rise as dark granite spires crowned with paler rock. On a still morning the reflection doubles the mountains, and the wind that normally ruins everything eases off for an hour or so.

From here a catamaran crosses to Paine Grande at the western end of the lake, which is how hikers start the W trek, and watching their rucksacks go aboard is a reminder that this is a place built around people on foot. For a rider the interest is the road. The park's main route is mostly gravel, firm in dry weather and washboarded where the traffic is heaviest, with long straights and abrupt dips where streams cross. The wind in Patagonia is not a weather feature but a permanent resident, and it can push a bike across the lane without warning, particularly on exposed crests. Keep your speed down and your grip relaxed.

A short walk from the car park leads to Salto Grande, where the water from Lake Nordenskjöld pours into Pehoé over a modest drop. It is not tall, but the volume is impressive, and the spray hangs in the cold air. You will often see guanacos, the wild relatives of llamas, grazing on the steppe nearby, and rheas, the small South American ostrich, sometimes stalk along the verge. Condors circle on thermals above the ridges when the weather allows.

Torres del Paine is a national park with an entrance fee and rules about where to go and when, so bring your passport and be ready for a ranger at the gate. Basic food is available at refugios and small lodges, but expect high prices.

Light is the gift here. Dawn and the hours before sunset bring warm tones on the rock, while midday can be flat and harsh. Dress for four seasons in a day.
t.grey lake@-51.1,-73.2:
Lago Grey is the park's glacial lake, and unlike the warm-looking blues elsewhere in Torres del Paine it is cold grey-green, scattered with icebergs that have calved from the Grey Glacier at its far end. The glacier is an outlet of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, the largest mass of ice in the southern hemisphere outside Antarctica, and the bergs drift down the lake on the wind, some as blue as sapphire, some striped with dust and sediment. They wash up on a beach of dark pebbles near the lodge, where you can stand close enough to hear them crackle.

The approach is the best part of the day. The road from the main park route runs west over gravel, passing small lakes, then dropping through windswept scrub toward the shore. Views of the Cuernos stay with you for much of the way, and on a clear morning the whole massif seems to float above the plain. The surface is variable, so take it gently, and be careful on wet days when the clay turns slick. The wind often funnels along the shore, making it hard to stay upright on the bike when you stop, so park with some thought.

Boat trips run to the glacier front from near the lodge, and walkers can follow a trail to a viewpoint above the beach. Even if you do neither, a walk along the pebbles with the icebergs at your feet is worth the cold. The ice has been retreating in recent decades, but the scale is still enormous, and the roar of a calving face can reach you across the water.

Wildlife in the area includes foxes, guanacos and the occasional puma, which locals say is more common than it used to be, though you are unlikely to see one. The southern beech forest in the sheltered folds of the land is a mix of lenga and ñire, turning copper and red in autumn, which is a strong reason to visit in March or April.

The nearest pumps are in Puerto Natales, so the same rule applies as elsewhere in the park: leave town with a full tank. The hotel by the lake offers meals and coffee, and the cold wind makes a hot drink very welcome.
t.crown terrace@-45.0,168.8:
Crown Terrace is a flat shelf of farmland high above the Arrow River, a wide green apron tipped against the Crown Range, and the first place on the road up from Queenstown where you can breathe out. Behind you the Wakatipu basin falls away to the lake and the zigzag of the Remarkables. Ahead, the tussock-covered slopes of the range rise in folds, brown in summer and white in winter. Sheep, cattle and deer graze the paddocks, and the roadside fences are lined with hawthorn, poplars and old stone walls. On a clear, still morning the light here is brilliant, and the air smells of cut grass and dry earth.

The road onto the terrace is the old Crown Range road, which leaves the main highway near Arrow Junction and climbs in a long series of bends, with the gradient easing as you reach the flat. Arrowtown, a few kilometres below, was a gold rush town in the 1860s, when the Arrow river gave up a fortune in gold to miners from all over the world, including many from China, whose stone huts you can still see on the edge of town. The terrace was a farming settlement above it, supplying the miners with meat and produce, and farming has remained the main business since.

For a rider, the terrace is a pleasant interlude. The road is well sealed, wide and open, with good visibility and very little traffic except for the occasional farm vehicle or tour van. The bends are gentle, and the views of the mountains are constant. The weather can change quickly, and a bright morning can turn to wind and rain by lunchtime, with snow on the tops even in summer. In winter, the road can be icy, and frost lingers in the shade, so take extra care on the bends.

Queenstown, about twelve kilometres away, is the place to buy fuel, food and anything else you need, and Arrowtown has a few small stations and shops, a good bakery and several cafés. There are no services on the terrace itself, but the surrounding farmland is a good place to pull over, watch the clouds roll across the range, and decide whether the day's riding will be dry. Take a windproof jacket, and fill the tank before you leave town.
t.crown range summit@-45.0,168.9:
The Crown Range summit reaches 1,121 metres, which makes this the highest paved main road in New Zealand, and it earns the title with a steep, twisting climb out of the Wakatipu basin. From the lookout at the top, the whole country seems to fall away: to the south, the Wakatipu basin and the jagged line of the Remarkables, and to the north the bare brown folds of the Cardrona valley, with Wanaka's lake beyond. The land is tussock and rock, treeless and bleached by wind, and the sky is enormous. Snow lies on the tops from May to October, and sometimes lingers into December.

On the Queenstown side, the road climbs in a famous series of hairpins known as the Zigzag, and a viewing area gives you a place to stop and look back at the road you have just climbed. The bends are tight, with a good surface and clear signs, and the gradient is steady. Going up, the temperature drops, and the wind picks up, and you feel the weather change. On the far side, the road falls more gently towards Cardrona, in long, open bends with views across the valley. It is a very satisfying ride, whichever way you do it.

The road is worth a little caution. In winter it can be snowy or icy, chains are often required, and the road is closed in bad conditions, so check the road status before you go. Even in summer, a cold wind can make a bright day feel raw, and mist can drop on the top without warning. Take warm layers, whatever the forecast says. The road is narrow in places, and tour buses and camper vans use it in numbers, so be patient and watch your mirrors.

Gold miners opened the first tracks over the range in the 1860s, and the pass was an important link between the Queenstown goldfields and the Cardrona and Wanaka areas. The modern road is now a popular scenic route as well as a commuter road for those who live in Wanaka and work in Queenstown. There is a car park and a lookout, but no café or toilet. Bring a flask and enjoy the view.
t.cardrona@-44.9,169.0:
Cardrona is a handful of buildings in a bare valley below the Crown Range, and it is one of the best-preserved relics of the Otago gold rush. In the 1860s the valley held thousands of people, with stores, hotels, a school and a brewery, all of them chasing gold in the river gravels. The rush faded, the crowds left, and the town shrank to almost nothing. What remains is the Cardrona Hotel, a white wooden building with a verandah that has stood since 1863 and still serves meals and drinks, along with a few old buildings and the remains of the diggings. The place has the unmistakable feel of a ghost town that has been revived, and the hotel's open fire is welcome on a cold day.

A short way along the road is the famous Bra Fence, a roadside wire fence hung with hundreds of bras, which began as a prank in the late 1990s and has grown into a curious roadside attraction. Whatever you think of it, it is a conversation starter. Nearby are a distillery that offers tastings, and the Cardrona Alpine Resort, one of the main ski fields of the region, which draws thousands of skiers and snowboarders from June to October.

The road here is part of the Crown Range route, and the ride down from the summit into Cardrona is superb. The road descends in long, flowing bends with wide views over the valley, the surface is good, and the traffic is light outside the ski season. In winter the road can be icy, and ski traffic is heavy at weekends, with cars towing trailers and tourist coaches. The weather can change quickly, and wind and cold are common even in summer.

The valley is dry and tawny, covered in tussock and scattered with schist rock, and the light is clear and sharp. Fuel is not available in Cardrona. The nearest places are Wanaka, to the north, with all the services a rider could want, and Queenstown, to the south, and it is wise to start with a full tank. The hotel serves a good meal, and the coffee at the roadside is welcome. If you have time, stop at the old cemetery and read the headstones, a reminder of the hard life of the miners.
t.haast pass@-44.1,169.4:
Haast Pass is the lowest crossing of the Southern Alps, at 562 metres, and the road over it carries State Highway 6 from the inland lakes of Otago to the wild West Coast. It is a gentle summit in a high, steep landscape, with beech forest on the slopes and snow peaks above, and it feels like a doorway between two worlds. On the east side, the land is dry and open, with tawny tussock and the pale blue of lakes. On the west side, the rain falls heavily, and the forest is dense, green and hung with moss, a temperate rainforest that reaches almost to the sea.

For centuries the pass was a route for Māori, who crossed it to bring back pounamu, the greenstone, from the rivers of the West Coast. European explorers found it in the 1860s, but the road was not completed until 1965, and until then the West Coast was cut off from the south by a gap of wild country. Today the road is a fine ride, with long, smooth bends, a good surface and wide views of rivers and mountains. Several waterfalls are visible from the road, notably Fantail Falls and Thunder Creek Falls, both a short walk from the car park, and a number of small bridges cross the roaring Haast River.

Weather is the main factor. Rain can fall in great quantity on the western side, and in winter the pass can have snow or ice, with chains required. Landslides and floods sometimes close the road, so check the status before you set out. Sandflies are a feature of the area, tiny biting insects that appear in clouds when you stop, so carry repellent, and do not be surprised if you leave with a few itchy bites. The ride is quiet, with moderate traffic, though in summer campervans and tourist cars are common.

Fuel is the key concern. There are long gaps between stations, and you should fill up in Wanaka or Queenstown before you start, and again at Haast, on the far side, if the tank is low. Makarora, on the east side, is a small settlement with limited services, and it is best not to rely on it. Take food and water, and give yourself time to stop at the waterfalls and the river. It is a day of beautiful scenery, and the best of it comes in the morning light.
t.blue pools@-44.2,169.3:
The Blue Pools are a spot on the Makarora river where meltwater from the Southern Alps runs clear and still over smooth, round stones, and the colour is something between sapphire and turquoise. A short walk of about fifteen minutes from the road leads through beech forest to a swing bridge across the river, from which you look down into deep, glassy pools where trout hang in the current. The water is so clear that the stones on the bottom seem within reach, and the colour changes with the light and the weather. After rain, the river turns a milky grey, and the pools lose their magic, so a dry spell is best.

The bridge is a favourite for swimmers, who jump from it in summer, though the water is bitterly cold, since it comes straight off the glaciers. The pool is deeper than it looks, but the current and the cold can be dangerous, and swimmers should take care. A rider in leathers may prefer to sit on the shore and watch. The forest here is silver and red beech, with ferns on the ground and moss on every trunk, and in the morning the air is cool and smells of damp earth and leaves.

The Makarora valley is a wild, beautiful place, within Mount Aspiring National Park, and it is a good base for walks, flights over the mountains and jet boat trips. The road along the valley is State Highway 6, and it is among the finest rides in the country. The surface is smooth, the bends are long and easy, and the views of the river and mountains are constant. Traffic is moderate, with campervans and tourists in summer, but it is rarely frantic. Mist and rain are common, so keep your visor clear and carry waterproofs.

The car park at the start of the track is small, and in peak season it can be crowded, so arrive early or late. Fuel is a matter for planning: the small settlement of Makarora, close to the pools, may have limited supplies, so rely instead on Wanaka, an hour or so back toward the lakes, and fill up there before you set out. Bring repellent for sandflies, which swarm the place on still days, and a camera. A short walk and a quiet half hour here will refresh any rider.
t.lake hawea@-44.6,169.3:
Lake Hawea is a deep glacial lake about thirty kilometres long, lying in a valley carved by ice between the dry hills of Central Otago, and the colour of it is the first thing you notice: a cold, dark blue, almost black in the middle, fading to emerald in the shallows. It sits just east of its twin, Lake Wanaka, separated from it by a narrow ridge called The Neck, and both were scooped out by the same great glaciers that once filled the valleys. The hills around are brown tussock and bare schist, with scattered willows and poplars along the shore, and in autumn the colours are gold and orange against the blue water.

The road, State Highway 6, runs along the eastern shore from the small town of Hawea to the lake's head, and then over the Haast Pass to the West Coast. The ride along the water is easy and rewarding, with gentle bends, good sealed surface and wide, open views. The lake level was raised in the 1950s for a hydro scheme, which is why the shoreline road sits close to the water in places. On a calm morning the surface mirrors the mountains, and the whole valley seems to hold its breath. Quebec City is the only walled city north of Mexico, and the old town, perched on a rock above the St Lawrence, still has the feel of a French provincial capital transplanted to North America. The Château Frontenac, the grand hotel with its copper roofs that dominates the skyline, was built in 1893 and is among the most photographed hotels in the world.

History is everywhere. In 1759, on the Plains of Abraham just outside the walls, British forces under General Wolfe defeated the French under Montcalm in a battle that lasted barely half an hour and decided the future of Canada. Both commanders died of their wounds. The grassy plains are now a park used for picnics and concerts. The people here are proudly French-speaking, and you will hear a distinct accent and a good deal of humour. A few words of French go a long way.

The ride starts here and heads east along the north shore of the St Lawrence into Charlevoix, a region of folded mountains, meteor-crater geology and small villages. Route 138 climbs and dips along the river, with wide views of the water and Île d'Orléans, the island where farmers have grown strawberries and apples since the seventeenth century. Further on, Baie-Saint-Paul has art galleries and a lively food scene, and the roads near Les Éboulements are twisty and rewarding.

Riding in the old town itself is a different matter. Streets are cobbled and steep, and in rain the stones become treacherous. Parking a bike is easiest outside the walls, and the old town is best explored on foot. A funicular links the upper and lower town and is a good use of a few minutes.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city of this size, and the restaurants range from simple crêperies to grand dining rooms. Poutine, maple taffy and tourtière are local specialties. Summer is busy and festive, while winter brings deep snow and bitter cold that make riding impossible.
t.zhigulevsk@53.4,49.5:
Zhigulevsk lies at the foot of the Zhiguli Hills on the right bank of the Volga, where the river makes a huge loop called the Samara Bend. The hills rise from the water like a green wall, topped with limestone and forest, and they are the only real mountains for hundreds of kilometres of otherwise flat steppe. Within a short distance, the climate shifts, and the Zhigulis carry plants and animals found nowhere else, some of them relics of the ice age.

The town has a very twentieth-century origin. It was built in the early 1950s to house the workers who constructed the Zhiguli hydroelectric dam, one of the largest of the Volga cascade, which turned the river into a long reservoir known locally as the Kuibyshev Sea. Across the dam is Togliatti, the car city where the Lada was made, and the model once sold abroad under the name Zhiguli. The name has a famous second life too, as the Zhigulevskoye beer, brewed in Samara since the nineteenth century by an Austrian-born brewer, which became the Soviet Union's standard lager.

The landscape is the real attraction. The Zhiguli National Park covers much of the hills, with oak and pine forest, limestone cliffs, caves and views of the Volga from the high bluffs. The painter Ilya Repin spent summers in the village of Shiryaevo in the early 1870s while working on his most famous painting, Barge Haulers on the Volga, and the village has a museum in his honour. The cliffs along the bank there offer a long view over the river and the islands.

The roads in the hills twist and climb with steep short sections, and the forests are cool in summer. The surface varies from smooth asphalt on the main road to rough patches on the small routes. Traffic on the highways is heavy with trucks, but the mountain lanes are quiet during the week. Wild boar and deer appear on the roads at dusk.

Zhigulevsk has fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and it is a good base for exploring. Fish from the Volga, dried and smoked, is the local snack, and the markets sell honey and apples from the surrounding villages. Summer is hot and dry, and the best months are May and September, when the hills are green or golden and the air is clear.
t.wanaka@-44.7,169.2:
Wanaka is a lakeside town of about four and a half thousand at the southern end of Lake Wanaka, where the water is the colour of a glacier's thought and the mountains stack up behind in ranks. It has long been the quieter sibling to Queenstown over the hill, a place where people come to ski, tramp and sit on the shore, and a lot of them end up staying. The famous willow standing in the water near the lakefront is a tourist photo, but locals have been loyal to it for years.

Behind the town are the glacier-carved valleys leading to Mount Aspiring National Park and the peak called Tititea, or Mount Aspiring, a pyramid rising above 3,000 metres. The lake itself was gouged by a great ice tongue during the last glaciations, and the terraces and moraines around it still frame the landscape. In summer the hills are tawny and the water cold, in autumn the poplars and willows go gold, and in winter snow dusts the tops of the Pisa Range and the roads can ice in the shade.

For riders, Wanaka is the starting point for the Crown Range Road, one of the great climbs in New Zealand. It leaves the valley, passes the old Cardrona Hotel, a gold-rush survivor from the 1860s with a verandah made for a flat white, and then climbs in switchbacks to a summit of about 1,076 metres, the highest sealed main road in the country. The road down the other side to Arrowtown and Queenstown is a long, sinuous descent with the Wakatipu basin laid out below. It can ice or snow in winter, and chains are sometimes required, so check conditions. Surface is good, traffic is moderate with campervans, and the best hours are early or late when the light is low and the sun draws long shadows across the schist hills.

Fuel is straightforward in Wanaka, with several stations and a good run of cafes and bakeries along the waterfront and main street. Arrowtown, with a little over two thousand people, and Cromwell, with just over five thousand, are the next options, and the Cardrona valley is thin on services. Fill up before the Crown Range and bring layers, because the weather can flip within an hour.
t.los andes chile@-32.8,-70.6:
Los Andes sits at the foot of the real thing. The town lies in the Aconcagua valley in central Chile, at about eight hundred metres, among orchards of avocados, grapes and citrus, with the whole wall of the high Andes rising to the east. On a clear day, the snow-covered cone of Aconcagua, at 6,961 metres the highest mountain outside Asia, is visible not far beyond the border, a tilted white tooth above the lesser peaks. The town was founded in 1791 by the governor Ambrosio O'Higgins, the father of the independence hero Bernardo O'Higgins, as a stop on the route over the mountains.

That route is the reason the town matters. The Paso de los Libertadores, also known as Cristo Redentor, is the main road crossing between Chile and Argentina, linking Santiago and Valparaíso with Mendoza, and it follows an old mule track used for centuries by traders, soldiers and travellers. In 1817 General San Martín led an army of some five thousand men over the Andes by passes near here to attack the Spanish in Chile, one of the great military marches of history. A railway, the Transandine, once ran over the pass, until floods wrecked part of it in 1984.

The road from Los Andes climbs steadily up the valley and then reaches the famous Caracoles, a stack of switchbacks that lifts the road up a headwall with a long series of tight hairpins, passing the ski resort of Portillo before it reaches the border tunnel at about 3,200 metres. The surface is generally good, but the road is heavily used by trucks, and queues at the border can be long, sometimes hours. In winter, snow and avalanches close the pass regularly, sometimes for days, so check the status with the border authorities. The air is thin, the wind cold, and weather can change quickly.

Los Andes has about fifty-seven thousand people, so it has all the services you need: fuel, banks, supermarkets and hotels. It is the last place to fill up and to organise the paperwork for the border, including insurance and vehicle documents. Customs on the Chilean side are at the top of the pass, so allow plenty of time.

Pastel de choclo, a baked corn and beef pie, and a glass of local red wine make a fitting last meal in Chile.
t.bucaramanga@7.1,-73.1:
Bucaramanga is a big, hilly, surprisingly green city in the northern Andes, and for riders it is the doorway to one of the great canyons of South America. It lies at around a thousand metres on a plateau in the department of Santander, with some 570,000 people in the city proper and many more in the neighbouring towns of Floridablanca and Girón. People call it the city of parks, and the bulk of its trees and gardens do, in fairness, make the heat easier to bear.

The ride out is the reason you are here. From the city the road climbs to the high shelf of the Mesa de los Santos, passing through farming country and the small town of Los Santos, then drops away into the gorge of the Chicamocha. This is a canyon of real scale, a deep dry trench cut by the river through bare, tawny mountainsides that look more like Arizona than the Colombia of the postcards. Hairpins fall for long stretches, the views open without warning at each bend, and the road is generally good tarmac, though lorries on the descents and the occasional rockfall deserve respect. The canyon is hot and arid at the bottom, cooler and often cloudy at the top, so layers matter.

On the canyon rim there is a national park with a cable car that glides high over the gorge, a tourist attraction that is easy to mock and hard to resist once you are looking down on the river. The Guane people lived in this region before the Spanish, and the colonial town of Girón, a short ride from Bucaramanga, keeps white-walled streets and old stone churches that are well worth an hour.

Santander has a reputation for its food and its bluntness. Try a plate of local specialities and, if you are brave, the fried big-bottomed ants called hormigas culonas, a regional delicacy. Fuel is no problem in the city, where you can fill up easily before you go, but the canyon road has long stretches with little, so top up when you see the chance. Start early. The light on the canyon walls is best in the morning, and the afternoon traffic builds quickly.
t.uruk archaeological city@31.3,45.6:
Uruk is where the story of the city begins. Around 3500 BC, on the Euphrates plain in what is now southern Iraq, a settlement grew into a place of tens of thousands of people, with temples, workshops and a priestly administration, and within a few hundred years the people of Uruk had invented writing. The earliest clay tablets, pressed with simple signs for grain, beer and sheep, come from here, and cuneiform grew out of them. The city was also the home, in legend, of Gilgamesh, a king said to have built its walls, which ran for some nine kilometres and which the epic that bears his name describes with pride.

Today, the site is a vast field of low mounds and trenches in the flat desert, a few tens of kilometres from As-Samawah, and it is listed by UNESCO as part of the Ahwar of Southern Iraq. The remains of the White Temple, on a platform raised above the plain, are about five thousand years old, and the huge ziggurat of the god Anu dominates the skyline. The Euphrates once flowed past the city and has long since moved away, leaving the ruins in dry, hard ground that ripples with heat. Wind carries pale dust across the tracks.

The ride is long, flat and exposed. The road from As-Samawah runs across the plain through scrubby farmland and salt pans, with little shade and long straight stretches. Summer temperatures often exceed fifty degrees, and the tarmac is hard on tyres, so travel between November and March. Sandstorms can arise quickly, and in winter the roads can be waterlogged. Before you plan, check travel advice, because access to archaeological sites and security conditions differ and can change.

As-Samawah, a city of about 150,000, is the nearest place for fuel, food and lodging, about thirty-three kilometres away, and the sensible thing is to fill up there and carry water. There are no facilities at the site, and a guard may ask to see permission, so find out in advance how to visit. The marshes of southern Iraq, home to the Marsh Arabs and to water buffalo, lie further east, and make a wonderful side trip if conditions allow.
t.ghamari cave@33.5,48.3:
Khorramabad is the capital of Lorestan province, a city of about 330,000 people sitting at roughly 1,200 metres in a broad valley of the central Zagros Mountains, and it has been inhabited for a very long time. On a rock in the middle of the city stands Falak-ol-Aflak, a castle with Sasanian foundations and later additions, which today houses a museum of the region's archaeology, including the remarkable bronzes of Lorestan, decorated horse bits, pins and animal figures made by people who lived here three thousand years ago. Nearby, a number of caves, including Yafteh, have yielded stone tools of the Paleolithic, so people were here tens of thousands of years earlier.

The cave that gives this point its name lies on the edge of the city, and I cannot describe the interior with confidence, but the setting is typical of the Zagros: limestone ridges pocked with caves, springs at their feet, and oak woods on the slopes above. The Kashkan river runs through the valley, and the old Sasanian stone bridge, Pol-e Shapuri, still spans a dry bed. The Lur people, with their own language, music and tribal traditions, make up most of the population, and are known for their hospitality.

For riders, Lorestan is a pleasant surprise. The roads from Khorramabad toward Borujerd, Aligudarz and Dorud twist through green valleys and over high passes, often lined with oaks and wild pistachios, and the railway to Tehran passes through an astonishing series of tunnels and bridges built in the 1930s. In spring the slopes are green and covered in wildflowers, and in winter snow can close the passes. Summers are warm, but the altitude keeps nights comfortable.

Fuel and services are all in the city, with stations on the main roads, and many restaurants serving ash soup, grilled kebabs and fresh bread. Be careful on mountain roads, where trucks are slow and visibility can be limited by fog or dust. Local people are keen to talk, and a rider who stops will almost certainly be invited to share tea. Start early, and check road conditions in winter.
t.noumea@-22.3,166.5:
Nouméa feels like a small French provincial city that was picked up and set down on a Pacific peninsula, and the combination is oddly charming. About ninety thousand people live here, almost half the territory of New Caledonia, and the town sprawls around a set of bays on the south-western tip of Grande Terre, with the lagoon, the second-largest in the world by reputation, stretching out in the turquoise light.

You can read the layers of its past in a short walk. The French founded the settlement in the 1850s and it grew as a base for the penal colony and for the nickel industry that still shapes the island's economy. The place has a Melanesian Kanak heritage that is older than any of it, and the Tjibaou Cultural Centre, designed by Renzo Piano and set among the trees outside the centre, is one of the more interesting buildings you will see on a motorbike trip. Baguettes and strong coffee are everywhere, and the market in the morning is worth an early visit for fruit, fish and flowers.

For a rider the town is a starting line, and a busy one. The traffic leaving along the main road is heavy at rush hour, with roundabouts, scooters and drivers who treat lane markings as a suggestion. Once you are past the suburbs, though, the road settles into a long coastal run north-west towards Païta and then on to the interior plains of the west coast. The climate is tropical, humid in the wet season from roughly January to March and drier and more pleasant from about May to October. Cyclones can disrupt travel in the warm months, so check the forecast before committing.

Fuel and services are no problem at all in Nouméa. The city has a proper range of stations, shops and workshops, and Mont-Dore, just along the coast, adds more. After this, the supply thins out, and while the west coast has villages with pumps, it is wise to refill whenever you pass a station. Watch the speed limits, which are enforced, and keep an eye on dogs and cattle on rural stretches.

Eat well before you leave. French-Pacific cooking is a joy, with fresh fish, coconut and good bread, and the sun sets early near the equator, so plan your day accordingly.
t.saratov@51.5,46.0:
Saratov spreads along the high right bank of the Volga, a big, busy city of more than eight hundred thousand people that grew rich on grain and river trade. The old center climbs a series of terraces from the water, with leafy avenues, nineteenth-century mansions and a long pedestrian street, and the hills behind it, including Sokolovaya Gora, give wide views over the river and the flat plain on the far shore. The Volga here is nearly a kilometer wide, and a long road and rail bridge, among the longest in Europe when it opened in 1965, links Saratov to its neighbor Engels on the left bank.

The city has two moments of fame that deserve a mention. Yuri Gagarin, the first man in space, studied at an industrial school in Saratov and learned to fly at the local aeroclub, and when he returned to earth in April 1961, he landed by parachute in a field near the village of Smelovka, not far from Engels. A monument marks the spot, and Gagarin is a hero in the city. The other is the story of the Volga Germans. Catherine the Great invited German farmers to settle the steppe here in the eighteenth century, and Engels, across the river, was the capital of the Volga German Republic until Stalin deported its people in 1941. The memory survives in old buildings and family names.

The riding opens up outside the city. Along the river, the hills rise in chalk and sandstone, and the roads towards Khvalynsk wind through low ridges with views of the water. They are not alpine, but they are varied, with gentle bends, farm villages and old white churches. The surface is mixed, with good and bad patches, and distances are long and the land is open. Summer is hot and dry, with temperatures that can exceed thirty-five degrees, while spring and autumn are comfortable. Winter brings snow and strong winds across the steppe.

Services are no trouble in a city this size, with fuel stations at every junction, restaurants and repair shops. It is the sensible place to fill up and eat before heading into the quieter hill country.

Walk along the embankment in the evening, when the river catches the light and families come out. The Volga here has a presence that is hard to describe.
t.ulyanovsk@54.3,48.4:
Ulyanovsk was called Simbirsk until 1924, when it was renamed in honor of its most famous son. Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, better known as Lenin, was born here in 1870, and for decades the city was a place of Soviet pilgrimage, with a vast memorial complex and a museum in the family home. Many visitors are now more interested in a different literary figure. Ivan Goncharov, author of the novel Oblomov, was born in Simbirsk in 1812, and the lazy hero of his book is as much a part of Russian identity as any revolutionary. Nikolai Karamzin, the great historian, was also from this region.

The city lies on the high right bank of the Volga, at a point where the river has been widened into the huge Kuybyshev Reservoir. From the embankments and the viewpoints above the water, the scale of the river is striking, with a far shore barely visible on a hazy day. The old center, with its wooden merchant houses and a few elegant stone buildings, climbs a hill, and the long bridge across the water is a landmark. The city has about six hundred and forty thousand people and builds aircraft and cars, and its airport is a major freight hub.

For riders, the countryside to the north and east is the Volga Upland, a belt of high, rolling land cut by ravines, with oak woods, fields and small villages. The Sengiley hills, with their chalk slopes and steppe vegetation, offer fine views over the river, and the roads there are quiet, with bends and some good surfaces. Others are patchy and broken, and gravel appears on the smaller tracks. Summers are hot and dusty, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, and the best season is late spring and early autumn. Winter is long and snowy.

Services are straightforward. Fuel stations, shops and cafes are on every main street, and the city has repair shops. Isheyevka, a smaller town to the south, has the basics too.

Take a walk along the embankment in the evening. The reservoir turns copper in the setting sun, and the long bridge lights up.
t.barichara@6.6,-73.2:
Barichara is the kind of town that makes people use superlatives, and for once they are mostly justified. Founded in the early eighteenth century on a ledge above the Suárez river canyon in Santander, it has kept its colonial streets almost intact: whitewashed houses with red-tile roofs, wooden doors and balconies, and pavements of pale stone that glow in the evening light. The name is thought to mean a place of rest in the language of the old Guane people, and the town lives up to it. With about four thousand people, it is small enough to cross on foot in a few minutes.

The sandstone is the signature. The cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, a big, pale church built of local stone, stands on the main square, with its twin towers and a pair of dark old trees in front. The streets slope to the edges of the town, where the view opens across the canyon to the mountains, and artisans work in stone, leather and paper in small workshops. A walk along the old Camino Real to the village of Guane, an hour or two on cobbles through dry country, is the best way to feel the history.

The ride that brings you here crosses the Chicamocha Canyon, one of the deepest in the Americas, where the road clings to a wall of dry, eroded rock above a brown river. The bends are tight, the surface is mixed, and the trucks are slow, so patience is needed. The national park above the canyon has a cable car across the void. Down at river level the heat can be fierce, while up at Barichara the air is mild, so dress in layers.

San Gil, thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town and has fuel, supermarkets and repair shops, and is also Colombia's centre for rafting and paragliding. Barichara has small restaurants selling local food, including goat, and hormigas culonas, large fried ants that are a regional snack, which you may or may not try. The cobbles are steep and slippery, so walk the bike carefully if you must move it, and leave it parked. Evening is the best time, when the stone turns gold and the sound of church bells carries.
t.milford sound@-44.7,167.9:
Milford Sound is not a sound at all, but a fjord, carved by a glacier and flooded by the sea, in the far south-west of New Zealand. Steep cliffs rise from the water to over 1,200 metres, including Mitre Peak, a pyramid of rock that dominates the view, and waterfalls drop from the heights, especially after rain, when hundreds appear. The area is part of Fiordland National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, one of the wettest places in the world, with about 6,800 millimetres of rain a year. There is no town here, only a small terminal for cruises, a few buildings and a runway. Te Anau, the nearest town, is about 120 kilometres away.

The Milford Road is a legend among riders. It leaves Te Anau and follows the lake and the Eglinton Valley, a flat-bottomed glacial valley with beech forest and tussock, and then climbs towards the Homer Tunnel, a one-lane tunnel about 1.2 kilometres long, cut through solid rock, which took nearly twenty years to build and opened in 1953. It slopes steeply downwards, and traffic is controlled by lights. Beyond it, the road zigzags down to the fjord. The surface is good, but the road is narrow, and tour buses are common.

Also take warm and waterproof clothing, because the weather can change from sun to storm quickly. In winter and spring, avalanches threaten the road, and it is sometimes closed for days; check conditions before you set out. Chains may be required, and the Homer Tunnel is cold and wet. In summer, sandflies are fierce at the fjord, and insect repellent is a good idea.

The wildlife is memorable: kea, the mountain parrots, hang around the tunnel and the car parks, and they enjoy picking at bike seats and straps, so be careful. Fur seals bask on the rocks, bottlenose dolphins swim in the fjord, and the Fiordland crested penguin nests in the forest. A cruise on the water, which takes about two hours, gives you the scale of the cliffs. In rain, the waterfalls turn the fjord into something unforgettable.
t.santa teresa@-13.1,-72.6:
Santa Teresa is a village in the cloud forest of the Cusco region of Peru, in the valley of the Urubamba river, and it lies at the end of a long, rough road from the Sacred Valley. The village is small and rustic, set among coffee and fruit farms and surrounded by steep green mountains, and it is one of the main routes to Machu Picchu for those who do not want to take the train. Hot springs at Cocalmayo, a short distance from the village, are a popular place to relax, and the people here grow coffee, avocado and bananas. The nearest towns are Santa Ana and Ollantaytambo, a long way off.

The road from the highlands over the Abra Málaga pass, at about 4,300 metres, is spectacular. It climbs through high puna grassland, with snow peaks and llamas, and then drops through cloud forest to the jungle edge. The route is partly paved and partly gravel, with hairpins, landslides and river crossings, and in the rainy season, from November to March, it can be dangerous. Mist and rain are common, and the temperature changes from cold at the pass to hot and humid in the valley. Be careful on narrow bends, and watch for trucks and buses.

The history here is deep. The Inca built roads and terraces throughout the valley, and the route between Ollantaytambo and Machu Picchu was an important link. Many travellers walk from the hydroelectric plant along the railway to Aguas Calientes, a few hours away. Machu Picchu, built in the fifteenth century and abandoned after the Spanish conquest, was brought to the world's attention by Hiram Bingham in 1911. Tickets for the site are limited and must be booked ahead.

Fuel is a point of concern: carry enough from Cusco or Ollantaytambo, as pumps in the valley are rare, and stations at the roadside may sell fuel from bottles. In Santa Teresa, there are small hostels and cafes, and you can have fresh coffee, trout and fried bananas. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time to ride. At dawn, mist rises from the forest, and the quiet is only broken by birdsong.
t.paso de los libertadores point 5@-32.8,-:
At the head of the valley the road gives up on the open air and goes into the mountain. The Cristo Redentor tunnel runs under the pass, about three thousand two hundred metres up, and marks the boundary between Argentina and Chile. Just beside it, the old road goes over the top, a narrow, steep gravel route that was the original crossing, famous for the statue of Christ the Redeemer placed on the frontier in 1904 as a sign of peace between the two countries after a border dispute.

The border crossing is a serious business. Both customs and immigration are handled in a large complex on the Argentine side, and the queues can be long, especially on weekends and holidays. Bring passport, vehicle papers and any insurance documents, and allow a couple of hours at the worst times. Fuel is not sold here, so make sure your tank is adequate, and do not expect much more than a snack bar.

The weather at this height is harsh. Even in midsummer, temperatures can drop and a storm can blow in without warning, and in winter the pass is often closed by snow and avalanche risk. The authorities close it frequently, so check status before setting off; the mountain does not negotiate. If it is open, the ride up is a great experience, with the air thin, the light brilliant and the peaks all around. The surface is good, with a few rough patches near the tunnel.

Think about altitude as well. A fast climb from Mendoza can make you tired and give you a headache, and a bike may run richer and weaker in thin air. Take it slowly, drink water, and rest if you need to. If you go over the old road when it is open, you will find a rewarding detour for photographs, with the statue standing alone against the sky. On the Chilean side, the road drops through a dramatic series of hairpins, and the reward is a warm, green valley far below.
t.milford road point 2@-45.0,168.0:
In the middle of the Milford Road the world becomes a valley of beech trees. Around these coordinates the highway runs along the floor of the Eglinton Valley, a wide, flat, glacier-carved trough with steep forested walls and silver tussock flats in between, and the quiet is startling after the traffic of the town. The air is clean and cool, and the light is soft, especially early in the morning, when mist hangs between the trees.

The valley is a place of mirrors. Small lakes lie beside the road, and on a still day they reflect the mountains with such clarity that you can hardly tell which way is up. The best known are the Mirror Lakes, a short boardwalk from the highway, where a signboard is cheerfully placed upside down so that you can read it in the water. Early morning is the best time, before the wind rises and the tour buses arrive, and the effect is wonderful.

For a rider, this section is a gift. The road runs straight and level for long stretches, with gentle bends and a good surface, giving time to look around and relax. Speed limits are low and strictly enforced, and campervans and buses often travel slowly, so overtaking opportunities are limited and caution is needed. Watch for wildlife, including deer, possums and the cheeky kea parrots, and for tourists stopped on the road to take photographs. In winter, frost and ice can linger in the shade until midday.

The beech forest is a living museum of Gondwana. Silver, red and mountain beech grow in tall stands, draped with moss and lichen, and the birdlife is rich, with tomtits, robins, bellbirds and the noisy fantail darting between trees. Mountain peaks, still bearing the scars of glaciers, rise on both sides, and in spring and early summer, waterfalls pour off the cliffs after rain. Campgrounds run by the Department of Conservation line the valley, offering a simple, quiet place to stay.

Basic toilets and picnic areas are scattered along the way, and there are few other facilities. Mobile coverage is limited or absent, so let someone know your plans. Sandflies can be fierce at the lakes, so bring repellent.
t.milford road point 3@-45.0,168.1:
The valley here is still the Eglinton, but with each kilometre the mountains grow closer and darker. The road runs along the river, which tumbles over gravel beds in braided channels, and the forest gives way in places to wide open flats of golden tussock, where deer graze at dusk. The peaks on either side are streaked with snow for much of the year, and on a clear day their reflections shimmer in the ponds and pools beside the road.

This was once the bottom of a glacier. Ice poured down from the high country thousands of years ago and scooped out the valley into the characteristic U-shape you can see in the cross-section, with sides so steep that the forest clings to them like a tapestry. The flat floor is covered in river gravel and tussock, and the pattern of braided streams shifts each time the river floods. Rock falls and avalanches are a regular feature of this landscape, which is why the road is sometimes closed.

For riders, this section offers a restful rhythm. The surface is good, the corners are gentle, and the road follows the contours of the valley, giving long views ahead. The wind can be strong, funnelled between the mountains, and gusts can push a loaded bike sideways. Rain squalls come up the valley without warning, and the temperature can drop sharply as you gain height. Keep your speed down, partly because limits apply and partly because deer and possums and sometimes people step onto the road.

The Department of Conservation manages the area, and walking tracks lead from the road to lakes, waterfalls and viewpoints. Lake Fergus, Lake Gunn and other small lakes are surrounded by forest, and the walking tracks around them are short and easy. The Divide is the low point in the mountains where the road finally gets over, and it is more modest than the name suggests. At about 530 metres above sea level, the saddle is the lowest pass across the Southern Alps, and it marks the watershed between rivers flowing east and those flowing west to the fiords. A small car park here is the trailhead for the Routeburn, Greenstone and Key Summit tracks, and it is full of hikers with boots and packs, drinking tea from flasks.

From here the landscape changes. Beyond the saddle the forest thickens, the walls of the valley steepen and the road heads north toward the Hollyford, the Homer Tunnel and the fiords. The mountains are bigger and sharper, the rock is bare and grey, and waterfalls tumble from every ledge after rain. The air has a sharp, cold, mineral scent, and clouds often tear across the peaks, revealing and hiding them in quick succession.

The riding becomes more serious. The road climbs toward the tunnel through a series of bends, with steep walls on one side and a drop on the other, and in winter the upper sections need chains and care, as avalanche risk is real. The surface can be wet and shaded, so ride within your limits and keep your distance from the vehicle in front. Rockfall and debris sometimes lie on the road, and the weather can close in rapidly, bringing rain, sleet or snow even in summer.

The Divide and the nearby Key Summit are also places of geological interest. From the summit, accessible by a steep walking track, three major valleys can be seen, draining to different coasts, and the alpine vegetation of tussock, mountain daisies and tiny cushion plants is a delight. The kea, the world's only alpine parrot, lives in this area, and is famous for its curiosity and its appetite for rubber and leather, so do not leave gloves or bike parts unattended.

Fill up at Te Anau before setting out, and carry a warm layer and waterproofs. Sandflies are present, so repellent is wise. Allow time to stretch with a short walk on the track, and enjoy the fresh mountain air before the final push.

At the end of the Milford Road the mountains seem to stand straight up out of the sea. The road emerges from the Homer Tunnel, a rough, unlit passage about 1.2 kilometres long, cut through solid granite and opened in 1953 after construction that began in the 1930s with picks, shovels and wheelbarrows. The tunnel drops steeply on the far side, and the road descends in a series of hairpins down the valley of the Cleddau River toward the sound.

The tunnel needs respect. Traffic is controlled by lights at busy times, and queues can build in summer, so be ready to wait. Inside, the surface is rough and wet, the gradient is steep, and the walls are bare rock with no lining in places. Keep your lights on, your speed low and your distance generous, and be alert for oncoming vehicles. Kea parrots gather at the entrance and are notorious for tearing at rubber, seats and anything loose, so keep an eye on your bike while you wait.

Milford Sound is a misnomer, because it is a fiord, carved by glacier, not a sound carved by river. It was named by a sealer after Milford Haven in Wales. Mitre Peak, a pyramid of rock rising nearly 1,700 metres from the water, dominates the view, and waterfalls fall from the cliffs after rain, sometimes in their hundreds. The water is dark, cold and still, and boat cruises set off from the terminal several times a day, a worthwhile way to see the scale of the place.

The road itself is quiet in the early morning and evening, when most tour buses are gone, and the return in late light is memorable. Be careful of tired drivers and tourists who are unfamiliar with the road.

Rain is the rule rather than the exception, with Milford among the wettest inhabited places on earth. Waterproofs are essential, and a dry change of gloves is a luxury worth packing. In fine weather, the view is unforgettable, and in rain, the waterfalls are even more spectacular. Sandflies are fierce here, so repellent is a good idea.
